items.title: Fixed-collar extension of C1alpha conductivities

references.title: Caro, García and Reyes, Stability of the Calderón problem for less regular conductivities
references.locator: Section 2, coefficient extensions; here the fixed background collar permits direct extension instead of a Whitney construction.

items.statement:
Let $d\ge3$ and let $\gamma\in X_d(R)$ for the domain, collar, ellipticity bounds and exponent $0<\alpha<1$ defining that class. Extend $\gamma$ by $1$ outside $\Omega$, using its continuous representative on $\overline\Omega$. Then $\gamma_e\in C^{1,\alpha}(\mathbb R^d)$, $\gamma_e-1$ has support contained in $\overline{\Omega'}$, and
$$\min\{m,1\}\le\gamma_e\le M,\qquad \sup_{\mathbb R^d}|\gamma_e|\le\max\{R,1\},\qquad \sup_{\mathbb R^d}|\partial_j\gamma_e|\le R,\qquad [\partial_j\gamma_e]_{C^{0,\alpha}(\mathbb R^d)}\le R.$$
Here the Hölder seminorm is $[f]_{C^{0,\alpha}}:=\sup_{x\ne y}|f(x)-f(y)|/|x-y|^\alpha$, and $j=1,\ldots,d$.
items.facts:
**Given:** A member $\gamma\in X_d(R)$ with $d\ge3$.

[F1] The class has $\gamma\in C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$, each first derivative has supremum and Hölder seminorm at most $R$, $m\le\gamma\le M$ almost everywhere, $M\ge1$, and $\gamma=1$ almost everywhere outside $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$. ([[def-ip-calderon-admissible-conductivity-class]])

proof_rows.text: Since $\overline{\Omega'}$ is compact in $\Omega$, every boundary point of $\Omega$ has a neighborhood disjoint from $\overline{\Omega'}$. On the open set $\Omega\setminus\overline{\Omega'}$, continuity and the almost-everywhere background condition force $\gamma=1$ everywhere: otherwise a sufficiently small ball would have positive measure and $|\gamma-1|$ bounded below by a positive number. Thus $\gamma_e$ is identically $1$ in a neighborhood of every boundary point and is $C^1$ globally. Its derivatives vanish off $\Omega$ and near $\partial\Omega$. The same continuity argument promotes the almost-everywhere ellipticity bounds to pointwise bounds in $\Omega$, and the extension gives the claimed global value and derivative bounds. It also shows $\gamma_e-1=0$ outside $\overline{\Omega'}$.

For $x,y\in\Omega$, the Hölder estimate for each derivative follows from [F1]. For $x,y\notin\Omega$, both derivatives are zero. In the remaining case take $x\in\Omega$ and $y\notin\Omega$. The segment from $x$ to $y$ has a first exit point $z\in\partial\Omega$, with $|x-z|\le|x-y|$. By step 1.1, $\partial_j\gamma_e(z)=\partial_j\gamma_e(y)=0$. Applying the original Hölder estimate on $\overline\Omega$ to $x,z$ gives $|\partial_j\gamma_e(x)-\partial_j\gamma_e(y)|\le R|x-z|^\alpha\le R|x-y|^\alpha$. These cases exhaust all pairs, establishing the global seminorm and hence $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity.

items.title: Rough conductivity Alessandrini identity and constant-quotient norm

references.title: Caro, García and Reyes, Stability of the Calderón problem for less regular conductivities
references.locator: Section 1 weak DN map convention and Section 2, Lemma 2.1 proof; the conductivity identity follows directly from weak solutions without extra coefficient regularity.

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$, $d\ge2$, be a nonempty bounded connected smooth domain, and let $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ be real measurable conductivities with $0<m\le\gamma_j\le M<\infty$ almost everywhere. Put $\mathcal D=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ and $E=\mathcal D/\mathbb C\mathbf1$, both with their quotient norms. For $f_j\in\mathcal D$, let $u_j$ be the weak $\gamma_j$-conductivity solution with trace class $f_j$. Then
$$((\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1)(f_2)=\int_\Omega(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)\nabla u_1\cdot\overline{\nabla u_2}\,dx.$$
The exact norm equality
$$\|\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2}\|_{\mathcal L(\mathcal D,\mathcal D^*)}=\|\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_2}\|_{\mathcal L(E,E^*)}=:\delta$$
holds, and consequently the integral above has absolute value at most $\delta\|[f_1]\|_E\|[f_2]\|_E$, and at most $\delta\|u_1\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\|u_2\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$. Here $[f_j]$ denotes the coset modulo constants; the stars denote continuous conjugate-linear duals.
items.facts:
**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, the domain and conductivities in the statement, and trace classes $f_1,f_2\in\mathcal D$.

[F1] The energy form is $a_j(v,w)=\int_\Omega\gamma_j\nabla v\cdot\overline{\nabla w}\,dx$, and $(\Lambda_{\gamma_j}f)(g)=a_j(u_{j,f},V_g)$ for every representative $V_g$ of $g$. The quotient norm of $[f]\in E$ is $\inf_{c\in\mathbb C}\|f+c\mathbf1\|_{\mathcal D}$. ([[def-ip-calderon-weak-dn-map-for-bounded-conductivities]])

[F2] Each trace class has a unique weak conductivity solution, $a_j(u_{j,f},z)=0$ for every $z\in H_0^1$, and the bounded DN map kills constants and annihilates constant test classes. ([[lem-ip-calderon-rough-dn-map-wellposedness]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are assumed at [F1]–[F2]. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

proof_rows.text: Let $v$ be the weak $\gamma_2$ solution with trace class $f_1$, available by [F2]. The difference $u_1-v$ belongs to $H_0^1$. The real-valuedness of $\gamma_2$ makes $a_2$ Hermitian, so $a_2(u_1-v,u_2)=\overline{a_2(u_2,u_1-v)}=0$. By the representative independence in [F1], $((\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1)(f_2)=a_1(u_1,u_2)-a_2(v,u_2)=a_1(u_1,u_2)-a_2(u_1,u_2)$. Subtraction of these two integrals is precisely the asserted conductivity identity. All integrals are absolutely convergent since the coefficients are bounded and the solution gradients are square integrable.

Set $T=\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2}$ and $b(f,g)=(Tf)(g)$. By [F2], $b(f+c\mathbf1,g+c'\mathbf1)=b(f,g)$ for all constants $c,c'$. If $N=\|T\|_{\mathcal L(\mathcal D,\mathcal D^*)}$, then $|b(f,g)|\le N\|f+c\mathbf1\|_{\mathcal D}\|g+c'\mathbf1\|_{\mathcal D}$. Taking the two infima independently gives $|b(f,g)|\le N\|[f]\|_E\|[g]\|_E$, including zero quotient norms. Thus the descended form has norm at most $N$. Conversely, the quotient map has norm at most one, so a bound $|b(f,g)|\le N'\|[f]\|_E\|[g]\|_E$ implies $|b(f,g)|\le N'\|f\|_{\mathcal D}\|g\|_{\mathcal D}$. Taking suprema over the two unit balls gives $N\le N'$. The operator norm into a conjugate-linear dual is exactly this supremum of absolute form values by the definition of the dual norm. Hence the two operator norms are equal.

The descended form in step 1.2 is exactly the difference of the two induced DN maps, so its norm is the stated $\delta$. Applying its form bound to step 1.1 proves the first integral bound. Since $u_j$ represents $f_j$, the two successive quotient infima give $\|[f_j]\|_E\le\|f_j\|_{\mathcal D}\le\|u_j\|_{H^1}$. Multiplying these inequalities proves the second bound, with no coefficient-dependent norm conversion factor.

items.title: Uniform cutoff estimates at the CGO characteristic sphere

references.title: Haberman and Tataru, Uniqueness in Calderón's problem with Lipschitz conductivities
references.locator: Section 2, Lemmas 2.1–2.2 and complete proofs, printed pp. 4–7.

items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge3$, $s\ge1$, and let $e_1,e_2\in\mathbb R^d$ be orthonormal. Put $\zeta=s(e_1-ie_2)$ and
$$p_\zeta(\xi)=-|\xi|^2+2i\zeta\cdot\xi.$$
Use the unitary angular-frequency Fourier transform $\widehat u(\xi)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\int e^{-ix\cdot\xi}u(x)\,dx$, and set
$$\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^b}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|p_\zeta(\xi)|^{2b}|\widehat u(\xi)|^2\,d\xi,\qquad \|u\|_{X_\zeta^b}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^d}(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)^{2b}|\widehat u(\xi)|^2\,d\xi.$$
For every fixed Schwartz function $\phi$, a constant $C=C(d,\phi)$ independent of $s,e_1,e_2$ satisfies, for all Schwartz $u$,
$$\|\phi u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{-1/2}}\le C\|u\|_{X_\zeta^{-1/2}},\qquad \|\phi u\|_{X_\zeta^{1/2}}\le C\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}.$$
Consequently
$$\|\phi u\|_2\le Cs^{-1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}},\qquad \|\nabla(\phi u)\|_2\le Cs^{1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}.$$
The norms are finite on Schwartz space; the values of the weights on the measure-zero characteristic sphere do not affect them. All four maps extend continuously to the completions in the respective input norms.
items.facts:
**Given:** Countable Choice and the parameters and Fourier norms in the statement.

[F1] Fourier transformation is unitary on $L^2$; the unitary angular convention is obtained from the library convention by $\widehat u(\xi)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\mathcal F_2u)(\xi/(2\pi))$. The Schwartz transform is Schwartz and transforms derivatives to $i\xi_j\widehat u$. ([[thm-plancherel]], [[thm-fourier-transform-maps-schwartz-space-continuously-to-itself]], [[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]])

[F2] Fourier transformation of a product of Schwartz functions is $(2\pi)^{-d/2}$ times convolution of their transforms. ([[thm-fourier-transform-of-a-product-under-an-integrable-transform-hypothesis]])

[F3] Nonnegative iterated integrals can be interchanged, polar integration is available in Euclidean subspaces, and the integral Cauchy–Schwarz inequality holds. ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]])

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed at the Fourier and integral interfaces. ([[def-countable-choice]])

proof_rows.text: Rotate coordinates so the two given vectors are the first coordinate vectors. Write $\xi=(a,se_2'+r\omega)$ with $a\in\mathbb R$, $r\ge0$, and $\omega\in S^{d-2}$ in the remaining coordinates. Then $p_\zeta(\xi)=s^2-a^2-r^2+2isa$, and its zero set is $\Sigma=\{a=0,r=s\}$. The upper bound follows by expanding $s^2-a^2-r^2$ and using $|a|+r+s\le C_Ks$. Also, if $|\xi|\ge8s$, the triangle inequality gives $|p_\zeta(\xi)|\asymp|\xi|^2$. Therefore $s/|p_\zeta(\xi)|\le C(1+D(\xi)^{-1})$ everywhere away from $\Sigma$.

The identity $p_\zeta(\eta)-p_\zeta(\xi)=|\xi|^2-|\eta|^2-2i\zeta\cdot h$ and the bound $|\xi|\le C(s+\sqrt{|p_\zeta(\xi)|})$ imply $$s+|p_\zeta(\eta)|\le C(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)\langle h\rangle^2.$$ For the auxiliary bound, use $|\xi|^2\le|p_\zeta(\xi)|+2\sqrt2s|\xi|$ and solve this quadratic inequality. In the difference identity, the terms $s|h|$, $\sqrt{|p_\zeta(\xi)|}|h|$, and $|h|^2$ are absorbed by the displayed right side using $s\ge1$ and $2ab\le a^2+b^2$. Since $\widehat\phi$ is rapidly decreasing, steps 1.1–2.1 now give $$\sup_\eta\int |\widehat\phi(\xi-\eta)|\frac{s+|p_\zeta(\eta)|}{|p_\zeta(\xi)|}\,d\xi\le C_\phi.$$ Indeed the integrand is bounded by $C_\phi\langle\xi-\eta\rangle^{-N}(1+D(\xi)^{-1})$ after choosing sufficiently many Schwartz powers.

For nonnegative weights $v,w$ positive almost everywhere and an integrable kernel $K$, Cauchy–Schwarz and Tonelli yield $$\int w(\xi)|(K*f)(\xi)|^2d\xi\le\|K\|_1\left(\sup_\eta\int |K(\xi-\eta)|\frac{w(\xi)}{v(\eta)}d\xi\right)\int v(\eta)|f(\eta)|^2d\eta.$$ To see this directly, bound $|K*f|^2$ by $\|K\|_1\int|K(\xi-\eta)||f(\eta)|^2d\eta$, multiply by $w$, and interchange nonnegative integrals. Apply this with $K=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\widehat\phi$, $v=(s+|p_\zeta|)^{-1}$ and $w=|p_\zeta|^{-1}$. Step 3.1 and [F2] prove the negative-half cutoff bound. The locally integrable singularity proved in step 2.1 and the quadratic large-frequency growth show that every Schwartz function has finite negative-half norm.

The positive-half estimate is the dual of step 4.1. More explicitly, use the same negative-half bound for the cutoff $\overline\phi$ and the Fourier $L^2$ pairing. Cauchy–Schwarz with reciprocal weights gives $|(\phi u,v)_{L^2}|=|(u,\overline\phi v)_{L^2}|\le\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}\|\overline\phi v\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}\le C\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}\|v\|_{X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. The supremum over Schwartz $v$ of the left side divided by its negative-half norm equals $\|\phi u\|_{X^{1/2}_\zeta}$. For this equality, truncate the weighted dual extremizer to a ball and away from $\Sigma$, approximate it by smooth compactly supported frequency functions there, and use ordinary $L^2$ density where the weights are bounded above and below; monotone truncation recovers the full weighted integral. Thus the claimed supremum uses no unattained extremizer.

The positive-half weight is at least $s$, so step 5.1 immediately gives $\|\phi u\|_2\le Cs^{-1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$. Split the gradient Fourier integral into $|\xi|\le8s$ and its complement. The first part has norm at most $8s\|\phi u\|_2$, hence at most $Cs^{1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$. On the complement $|\xi|^2\le C|p_\zeta(\xi)|$, so its norm is at most $C\|\phi u\|_{X^{1/2}_\zeta}\le C\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$. Since $s\ge1$, their sum gives the gradient bound. A bounded map sends norm-Cauchy sequences to norm-Cauchy sequences, with the same bound; passing to equivalence classes therefore extends each map uniquely to the stated completions.

items.title: Circle-averaged negative Bourgain estimate for rough vector fields

references.title: Haberman and Tataru, Uniqueness in Calderón's problem with Lipschitz conductivities
references.locator: Section 3, Lemma 3.1 and complete proof, printed pp. 9–13; the proof here retains explicit frequency dependence.

references.title: Caro, García and Reyes, Stability of the Calderón problem for less regular conductivities
references.locator: Section 3, equations (3.14)–(3.16), printed pp. 12–13.

items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge3$, $k\in\mathbb R^d$, and fix an oriented two-plane $P\perp k$. For a unit vector $\eta\in P$, let $\eta^\perp$ be its positive quarter turn. For $s\ge|k|/2$, put $r(s)=\sqrt{s^2-|k|^2/4}$ and
$$\zeta_\pm(s,\eta)=\pm s\eta+i(k/2\pm r(s)\eta^\perp).$$
These phases are null, have length $\sqrt2s$, and sum to $ik$. Use the unitary angular Fourier convention and the norms $\dot X_\zeta^b,X_\zeta^b$ with inhomogeneous weight $s+|p_\zeta|$, where $p_\zeta(\xi)=-|\xi|^2+2i\zeta\cdot\xi$. For a fixed $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, define
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f):=\frac1\lambda\int_{S^1(P)}\int_\lambda^{2\lambda}\|\phi\operatorname{div}f\|_{\dot X_{\zeta_\pm(s,\eta)}^{-1/2}}^2\,ds\,d\eta.$$
Here $d\eta$ is arclength, either sign can be used, and the derivative is distributional. For $\lambda\ge100\sqrt{1+|k|^2}$ and $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C^d)$,
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le C\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\|f\|_2^2,$$
where $C$ depends only on $d,\phi$. If $f\in H^1$, also
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le\frac C\lambda\|\nabla f\|_2^2.$$
Let $\rho\in C_c^\infty(B(0,1))$ be nonnegative with integral $1$, put $\rho_h(x)=h^{-d}\rho(x/h)$, and define $\omega_2(f,h)=\sup_{|y|\le h}\|f(\cdot-y)-f\|_2$. For $h>0$ one consequently has
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le C_\rho\left[\frac{\|f\|_2^2}{\lambda h^2}+\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\omega_2(f,h)^2\right].$$
items.facts:
**Given:** Countable Choice and the parameters, phases and vector field in the statement.

[F1] For any null phase of length $\sqrt2s$, multiplication by a fixed smooth compactly supported function maps $X^{-1/2}_\zeta$ to $\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta$ with norm independent of $s\ge1$ and the phase directions. ([[lem-ip-calderon-bourgain-cutoff-estimates]])

[F2] The angular Fourier transform preserves $L^2$ norms and sends the divergence to multiplication by $i\xi\cdot$. Nonnegative frequency and parameter integrals can be interchanged. ([[thm-plancherel]], [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])

[F3] Convolution with an $L^1$ kernel is bounded on $L^2$ by its $L^1$ norm. ([[thm-young-convolution-inequality]])

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed through [F1]–[F3]. ([[def-countable-choice]])

proof_rows.text: Direct expansion gives $\zeta_\pm\cdot\zeta_\pm=0$, $|\zeta_\pm|^2=2s^2$, and $\zeta_++\zeta_-=ik$. For either sign, writing $a=\xi\cdot\eta$, $b=\xi\cdot\eta^\perp$, the symbol satisfies $|p_\zeta(\xi)|\asymp\bigl||\xi|^2+k\cdot\xi\pm2r(s)b\bigr|+2s|a|$, with absolute constants. Put $R=|\xi|$, $A=|\Pi_P\xi|$, and $W(s,\eta,\xi)=R^2/(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)$. We prove the uniform kernel bound $\lambda^{-1}\int_{S^1}\int_\lambda^{2\lambda}W\,ds\,d\eta\le C(1+(1+|k|^2)/\lambda)$. If $R\le100\sqrt{1+|k|^2}$, the pointwise bound $W\le R^2/\lambda$ proves it. Otherwise $|k\cdot\xi|\le R^2/100$. If $A\le R^2/(100\lambda)$, then $2r(s)|b|\le4\lambda A\le R^2/25$ and the real part has absolute value at least $R^2/2$, giving $W\le2$. Thus only the case $A>R^2/(100\lambda)$ remains; here $R^2/A<100\lambda$.

In this last case, on $|a|\ge A/2$ the imaginary part gives $W\le R^2/(\lambda A)\le100$. On the remaining angular set, partition into shells $E_j=\{2^{-j-2}A<|a|\le2^{-j-1}A\}$, $j\ge0$, ignoring the measure-zero set $a=0$. Each shell has arclength at most $C2^{-j}$, since $a=A\cos\theta$ and $|\sin\theta|\ge\sqrt3/2$ there. On each shell, $|b|\ge\sqrt3 A/2$ and the denominator is bounded below, up to an absolute constant, by $|B\pm2r(s)b|+\lambda(1+2^{-j-1}A)$, where $B=R^2+k\cdot\xi$ is independent of $s,\eta$. Since $dr/ds=s/r\ge1$ and the $r$-interval is contained in $[\lambda/2,2\lambda]$, integration in $s$ is bounded by integration in $r$ over this latter interval. For any interval $I$ of length at most $2\lambda$ and $c>0$, splitting at the zero of the affine function gives $\int_I(|B+2br|+c)^{-1}dr\le C|b|^{-1}\log(1+\lambda|b|/c)$. Therefore $\int_\lambda^{2\lambda}W\,ds\le C(R^2/A)\log(1+C A/(1+2^{-j-1}A))\le C\lambda(j+1)$. Multiplying by the shell measure and summing $\sum_{j\ge0}(j+1)2^{-j}<\infty$ proves the kernel bound of step 1.1. This proof treats all $A$, including $A=0$ via its earlier case, and its constants are independent of $k,P$.

Initially let $f$ be Schwartz. By [F1], $\|\phi\operatorname{div}f\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}^2\le C\int |\xi\cdot\widehat f(\xi)|^2/(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)\,d\xi\le C\int W(s,\eta,\xi)|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi$. Interchange the nonnegative integrals using [F2] and apply step 2.1 and Plancherel. This proves the first estimate. For $f\in H^1$, the simpler denominator bound $s+|p_\zeta|\ge s\ge\lambda$ gives $\|\phi\operatorname{div}f\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}^2\le C\lambda^{-1}\|\nabla f\|_2^2$; averaging over the parameter interval of length $\lambda$ and circle length $2\pi$ proves the second estimate. The same estimates hold for general $L^2$ and $H^1$ fields by Fourier truncation and smooth approximation. The limits match the distribution $\phi\operatorname{div}f$: convergence in the weighted negative space implies distributional convergence when tested against Schwartz functions, by reciprocal-weight Cauchy–Schwarz, and $L^2$ convergence of $f$ already implies distributional convergence of its derivative.

Write $f=f_h+(f-f_h)$ with $f_h=\rho_h*f$. Differentiation under the convolution, first for smooth fields and then by $L^2$ approximation, gives $\|\nabla f_h\|_2\le\|\nabla\rho_h\|_1\|f\|_2=C_\rho h^{-1}\|f\|_2$ by [F3]. Also $\|f-f_h\|_2\le\omega_2(f,h)$: at each $x$ apply the integral Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to the probability density $\rho_h(y)dy$, then integrate in $x$ and interchange nonnegative integrals to bound the squared norm by $\int\rho_h(y)\|f-f(\cdot-y)\|_2^2dy$. The support of $\rho_h$ is inside $|y|\le h$. Since $\|v+w\|^2\le2\|v\|^2+2\|w\|^2$, apply the $H^1$ estimate of step 3.1 to $f_h$ and its $L^2$ estimate to $f-f_h$. This yields the claimed mollified estimate after enlarging the constant.

items.title: Quantitative CGO construction for C1alpha conductivity potentials

references.title: Haberman and Tataru, Uniqueness in Calderón's problem with Lipschitz conductivities
references.locator: Theorem 2.1 and proof, printed pp. 8–9; Section 4, Theorem 4.1 and contraction proof, printed pp. 13–14.

references.title: Caro, García and Reyes, Stability of the Calderón problem for less regular conductivities
references.locator: Section 3, equations (3.7)–(3.17), printed pp. 10–14.

items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Fix $d\ge3$, $0<\alpha<1$, a ball $B\subset\mathbb R^d$, and $K>0$. Let $\gamma\in C^{1,\alpha}(\mathbb R^d)$ be real and positive, equal to $1$ outside $B$, and put $a=\nabla\log\gamma$. Suppose
$$\|a\|_\infty+[a]_{C^{0,\alpha}(\mathbb R^d)}\le K.$$
Define the compactly supported distribution $q$ and its multiplication form by
$$\langle q,v\rangle=-\frac12\int a\cdot\nabla v+\frac14\int |a|^2v,\qquad \langle m_q u,v\rangle=-\frac12\int a\cdot\nabla(uv)+\frac14\int |a|^2uv.$$
These pairings are complex bilinear. For the angular Fourier norms with $p_\zeta(\xi)=-|\xi|^2+2i\zeta\cdot\xi$, there are constants $C,s_0\ge1$, depending only on $d,\alpha,B,K$, such that for every null phase $\zeta$ of length $\sqrt2s$ with $s\ge s_0$,
$$\|m_q\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}\to\dot X_\zeta^{-1/2}}\le Cs^{-\alpha/(1+\alpha)}\le\frac12.$$
There is $r_\zeta\in\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}\cap H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d)$ such that
$$U_\zeta(x)=e^{x\cdot\zeta}(1+r_\zeta(x)),\qquad (-\Delta+q)U_\zeta=0,\qquad \|r_\zeta\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}\le2\|q\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{-1/2}}.$$
The equation uses the multiplication form above against compactly supported smooth tests. For the phases $\zeta_\pm(s,\eta)$ associated to $k$ and $P\perp k$, if $\lambda\ge\max\{s_0,100\sqrt{1+|k|^2}\}$, then for either sign,
$$\frac1\lambda\int_{S^1(P)}\int_\lambda^{2\lambda}\left(\|q\|_{\dot X_{\zeta_\pm}^{-1/2}}^2+\|r_{\zeta_\pm}\|_{\dot X_{\zeta_\pm}^{1/2}}^2\right)ds\,d\eta\le C\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\lambda^{-\alpha/(1+\alpha)}.$$
items.facts:
**Given:** Countable Choice and the domain, exponent and conductivity in the statement.

[F1] For every fixed smooth compactly supported $\phi$, the cutoff estimates give $\|\phi u\|_2\le C s^{-1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$ and $\|\nabla(\phi u)\|_2\le Cs^{1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$. Also $\|\phi f\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}\le C\|f\|_{X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. ([[lem-ip-calderon-bourgain-cutoff-estimates]])

[F2] For a compactly supported vector field $f\in L^2$, the average of $\|\phi\operatorname{div}f\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}}^2$ is at most $C[(\lambda h^2)^{-1}\|f\|_2^2+(1+(1+|k|^2)/\lambda)\omega_2(f,h)^2]$. ([[lem-ip-calderon-averaged-negative-bourgain-estimate]])

[F3] Fourier transformation is unitary, and convolution maps $L^1\times L^2$ into $L^2$ with the product norm bound. ([[thm-plancherel]], [[thm-young-convolution-inequality]])

[F4] Distributional differentiation is defined by negative transposition on test functions, with complex bilinear pairing. ([[def-distributional-derivative]])

proof_rows.text: Fix $\phi\in C_c^\infty$ equal to $1$ on the ball consisting of points of distance at most $2$ from $B$. For Schwartz $u,v$, the integrands defining $m_q$ are supported where $\phi=1$, so they can be written using $u_B=\phi u,v_B=\phi v$. By [F1], $\|u_Bv_B\|_1\le Cs^{-1}\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}\|v\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$ and $\|\nabla(u_Bv_B)\|_1\le C\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}\|v\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$, the latter from the product rule and the two combinations $s^{1/2}s^{-1/2}$. Thus a bounded coefficient multiplying $u_Bv_B$ costs $Cs^{-1}$, whereas a bounded vector coefficient multiplying its gradient costs $C$. The same estimates hold when $u,v$ have any two null phases of the same length, because [F1] is uniform in the phase directions. These bounds also prove continuity of the bilinear form on the weighted completions and local $H^1$ representatives.

Choose a nonnegative smooth mollifier $\rho$ of integral $1$ supported in the unit ball and put $a_h=\rho_h*a$ for $0<h\le1$. The bounds $\|\operatorname{div}a_h\|_\infty\le C_\rho h^{-1}\|a\|_\infty$ and $\|a-a_h\|_\infty\le[a]_{C^{0,\alpha}}h^\alpha$ follow, respectively, by differentiation of the kernel and integration of $|a(x)-a(x-y)|\le K|y|^\alpha$. The support of $a_h$ stays inside the region where $\phi=1$. Split the derivative term of $m_q$ into $a_h$ and $a-a_h$, and integrate the former by parts. Step 1.1 gives $|\langle m_qu,v\rangle|\le C[s^{-1}K^2+s^{-1}h^{-1}K+Kh^\alpha]\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}}\|v\|_{\dot X^{1/2}}$. Take $h=s^{-1/(1+\alpha)}$; since $s\ge1$, this is bounded by $Cs^{-\alpha/(1+\alpha)}$ times the product of norms. Weighted Fourier duality identifies the bounded bilinear form with a map to $\dot X^{-1/2}$: in Fourier coordinates the dual weight is $|p_\zeta(-\xi)|^{-1}$ for a bilinear pairing, and reflection changes the test phase to $-\zeta$; the cutoff bounds of step 1.1 are identical for $\zeta$ and $-\zeta$. Therefore the same proof with $v$ measured in $\dot X_{-\zeta}^{1/2}$ gives exactly the asserted map norm. Enlarge $s_0$ until this norm is at most $1/2$.

The weighted completions are realized as the Fourier $L^2$ spaces with weights $|p_\zeta|^{\pm1}$: smooth functions supported away from the characteristic set and inside a bounded frequency ball are dense by truncation and ordinary $L^2$ approximation there. They define tempered distributions because reciprocal-weight Cauchy–Schwarz controls their pairing with a Schwartz test; the only new local singularity is $|p_\zeta|^{-1}$, integrable by the codimension-two computation in [F1]. Multiplication of the Fourier transform by $p_\zeta^{-1}$ is consequently an isometry $G_\zeta:\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta\to\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta$ and is a distributional right inverse of $\Delta+2\zeta\cdot\nabla$. The characteristic set has measure zero, so its values need not be assigned. Also $q\in\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta$: its compactly supported divergence part follows from [F1] applied to $\operatorname{div}a\in X^{-1/2}_\zeta$, and its bounded compactly supported zero-order part follows from the same cutoff bound. For the former, $|\xi|^2/(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)$ is bounded for fixed $s$, so $a\in L^2$ suffices; for the latter, the inhomogeneous negative norm is at most $s^{-1/2}$ times its $L^2$ norm.

By steps 2.1–3.1, the series $r_\zeta=\sum_{j=0}^\infty(G_\zeta m_q)^jG_\zeta q$ converges in $\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta$, has norm at most $2\|q\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$, and satisfies $(\Delta+2\zeta\cdot\nabla)r_\zeta=q+m_qr_\zeta$. For a cutoff equal to $1$ on any fixed compact set, [F1] gives convergence in $H^1$ there, so $r_\zeta\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. The product-form definition agrees with the distributional equation by this local convergence. Conjugating $-\Delta$ by $e^{x\cdot\zeta}$ gives $-\Delta-2\zeta\cdot\nabla-\zeta\cdot\zeta$; the last term vanishes. Hence the displayed remainder equation is exactly $(-\Delta+q)e^{x\cdot\zeta}(1+r_\zeta)=0$. This proves existence and the remainder bound.

Since $a$ is supported in $\overline B$, for $0<h\le1$ its translation difference has support in a fixed bounded ball and absolute value at most $Kh^\alpha$. Consequently $\omega_2(a,h)\le C_BKh^\alpha$ and $\|a\|_2\le C_BK$. Apply [F2] to $a$ with a cutoff equal to $1$ near its support. The zero-order part $|a|^2$ has squared negative-half norm at most $Cs^{-1}\||a|^2\|_2^2\le Cs^{-1}C_BK^4$ by [F1]. The inequality $\|v+w\|^2\le2\|v\|^2+2\|w\|^2$ therefore bounds the average squared norm of $q$ by $C[\lambda^{-1}+\lambda^{-1}h^{-2}+(1+(1+|k|^2)/\lambda)h^{2\alpha}]$. Set $h=\lambda^{-1/(2+2\alpha)}$. Both $\lambda^{-1}h^{-2}$ and $h^{2\alpha}$ equal $\lambda^{-\alpha/(1+\alpha)}$, and $\lambda^{-1}$ is no larger. The pointwise remainder bound from step 4.1 then gives the asserted average for $q$ and $r$ together. The parameterized norms and integrals are measurable: first for Fourier-truncated smooth data this follows directly from the measurable weights; the Neumann partial sums are measurable as iterated multipliers and fixed coefficient forms, and their norm limits retain measurability.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge3$, $0<\alpha<1$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected smooth domain, let $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, and fix $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$ and $R>0$. For every $\gamma,\gamma_0\in X_d(R)$ there exist constants $C>0$, $\rho>0$ and $t_0\in(0,1)$, depending only on $d,\alpha,\Omega,\Omega',m,M,R$, such that
$$\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C\,\omega\!\left(\|\dot{\Lambda}_\gamma-\dot{\Lambda}_{\gamma_0}\|_{\mathcal L(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1,(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1)^*)}\right),$$
where $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ is the trace quotient and $\dot\Lambda_\gamma$ is the induced weak Dirichlet-to-Neumann map on the constant quotient, and
$$\omega(0):=0,\qquad \omega(t):=\left[\log\!\left(\frac1{\min\{t,t_0\}}\right)\right]^{-\rho}\quad(t>0).$$

Extend both coefficients by $1$ using [F1], and fix a ball $B$ containing $[0,1]^d$ and a neighborhood of it. Put $g_j=\sqrt{\gamma_j}$ and $a_j=
abla\log\gamma_j$. These are globally $C^1$ and $C^{0,\alpha}$, respectively, and $a_j$ has support in $\overline{\Omega'}$. Their supremum and Hölder bounds are uniform: the positive lower bound $m_*:=\min\{m,1\}$ gives $|a_j|\le C_dR/m_*$; on $|x-y|\le1$, expand $
abla\gamma_j(x)/\gamma_j(x)-
abla\gamma_j(y)/\gamma_j(y)$, using the derivative Hölder bound and $|\gamma_j(x)-\gamma_j(y)|\le\sqrt dR|x-y|$; on larger distances use twice the supremum. Thus [F4] applies uniformly. Let $q_j=	frac12\operatorname{div}a_j+	frac14|a_j|^2$ and $Q=q_1-q_2$, with bilinear distribution pairings as in [F4].

The Liouville form identity is $\int
abla v\cdot
abla w+\langle q_j,vwangle=\int\gamma_j
abla(v/g_j)\cdot
abla(w/g_j)$ for $v,w\in H^1$ on a bounded set. Indeed $q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$ means $\langle q_j,vwangle=-\int
abla g_j\cdot
abla(g_j^{-1}vw)$; expanding this derivative gives the displayed identity term by term. All products are integrable since $g_j,g_j^{-1},
abla g_j$ are bounded and the factors are in $H^1$. The identity extends from smooth factors by local $H^1$ approximation; multiplication by a bounded $C^1$ function with bounded derivative is continuous on $H^1$, as follows from the product rule and the same approximation. Since $g_j=1$ near $\partial\Omega$, the trace of $U_j$ equals that of $u_j:=U_j/g_j$. A solution $U_j$ of the Schrödinger form equation therefore gives a weak conductivity solution $u_j$: test the form identity with $w=g_jz$, first for compactly supported tests and then in $H_0^1$ by density. Subtracting the two Schrödinger forms for solutions $U_1,U_2$, or repeating the weak-solution subtraction in [F2], gives $\langle Q,U_1U_2angle=((\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1)(\overline{f_2})$. Here $f_j$ is the trace class of $u_j$, and the conjugation converts the sesquilinear DN convention to the bilinear interior form. The compact support of $Q$ makes its whole-space pairing identical to its pairing on $\Omega$. Consequently $|\langle Q,U_1U_2angle|\le\delta\|u_1\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\|u_2\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$.

Use the paired phases $\zeta_\pm=s(\pm\eta)+i(k/2\pm\sqrt{s^2-|k|^2/4}\,\eta^\perp)$ of [F4]. For fixed $s$ their remainders satisfy $\|r_j\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_j}}\le C\sqrt s$. To verify this last uniform bound, the symbol inequality $|\xi|^2/(s+|p_{\zeta_j}(\xi)|)\le Cs$ follows by splitting $|\xi|\le8s$ and its complement. Apply the negative cutoff bound in [F3] to $\operatorname{div}a_j$ and $|a_j|^2$ as in [F4] to obtain $\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{\zeta_j}}\le C\sqrt s$. The two positive cutoff bounds then give $\|r_j\|_{L^2(B)}\le C$ and $\|\nabla r_j\|_{L^2(B)}\le Cs$. Multiplication by $g_j^{-1}e^{x\cdot\zeta_j}$ yields $\|u_j\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le Ce^{Cs}s$. Thus step 2.1 bounds the exact interior product by $C\delta e^{Cs}s^2$.

Fix a compactly supported smooth cutoff $\phi=1$ near $\overline{\Omega'}$. The cutoff proof in [F3] also gives $\|\phi e^{ik\cdot x}v\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}\le C\langle k\rangle^N\|v\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$ for a fixed integer $N=d+10$. In detail, its convolution bound uses a decay exponent greater than $d+3$ and the factor $\langle\xi-\eta\rangle^2$; replacing $\widehat\phi(h)$ by $\widehat\phi(h-k)$ increases the required weighted supremum by at most $C\langle k\rangle^{d+8}$, while its $L^1$ norm is unchanged. Taking square roots, and enlarging the exponent to $N$, proves the assertion via its positive-half dual bound. Since $q_j$ is real, $\widehat q_j(-\xi)=\overline{\widehat q_j(\xi)}$, and $p_{-\zeta}(\xi)=p_\zeta(-\xi)$, so $\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{-\zeta}}=\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz in the bilinear pairing therefore gives $|\langle q_j,e^{ik\cdot x}r_l\rangle|\le C\langle k\rangle^N\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{\zeta_l}}\|r_l\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_l}}$. For the quadratic term, expand the definition of $q_j$ on $e^{ik\cdot x}r_1r_2$ and use [F3] on each factor with its own phase. The product and differentiated product have $L^1$ norms at most $Cs^{-1}$ and $C$, respectively, times the two remainder norms. The derivative of the exponential adds $C|k|s^{-1}$, giving $|\langle q_j,e^{ik\cdot x}r_1r_2\rangle|\le C(1+|k|)\|r_1\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_1}}\|r_2\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_2}}$.

Since $\zeta_1+\zeta_2=ik$, expand $U_1U_2=e^{ik\cdot x}(1+r_1+r_2+r_1r_2)$ in step 3.1. Move the three remainder terms to the other side and apply step 4.1. Average over $\lambda\le s\le2\lambda$ and the unit circle in the fixed plane $P\perp k$, dividing by its total measure $2\pi\lambda$. The left side $|\langle Q,e^{ik\cdot x}\rangle|$ is independent of these parameters. For each linear or quadratic product, integral Cauchy–Schwarz and [F4] bound its average by $C\langle k\rangle^N(1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda)\lambda^{-\beta}$, where $\beta=\alpha/(1+\alpha)$. The same bound applies when the potential $q_j$ and remainder $r_l$ have different indices, because [F4] holds for either coefficient and either phase. Absorbing the fixed Fourier normalization gives $|\widehat Q(k)|\le C\delta e^{C\lambda}\lambda^2+C\langle k\rangle^N(1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda)\lambda^{-\beta}$ whenever $\lambda\ge\max\{s_0,100\langle k\rangle\}$. Replacing $k$ by $-k$ if needed accounts for the negative-sign Fourier convention.

Define $\mathcal Q:=\|(1+|\xi|^2)^{-1/2}\widehat Q(\xi)\|_2$. This is finite since $Q=\tfrac12\operatorname{div}(a_1-a_2)+\tfrac14(|a_1|^2-|a_2|^2)$ with both coefficient fields in $L^2$. For $t\ge1$, its low-frequency contribution is at most $Ct^{d/2}\sup_{|k|\le t}|\widehat Q(k)|$. The high-frequency contribution of the zero-order field is at most $Ct^{-1}$. For the divergence field $f=a_1-a_2$, split $f=\rho_h*f+(f-\rho_h*f)$ with a fixed nonnegative unit-mass mollifier. Plancherel bounds its high-frequency contribution by $Ct^{-1}\|\operatorname{div}(\rho_h*f)\|_2+\|f-\rho_h*f\|_2\le C(t^{-1}h^{-1}+h^\alpha)$. The last two bounds follow by differentiating the convolution kernel and by the uniform Hölder estimate with fixed compact support, exactly as in [F4]. Taking $h=t^{-1/(1+\alpha)}$ gives $\mathcal Q\le C[t^{d/2}\sup_{|k|\le t}|\widehat Q(k)|+t^{-\beta}]$.

Choose $A=2+(N+d+1)/\beta$ and a fixed $L\ge\max\{s_0,200\}$. Set $\lambda=Lt^A$. Then $\lambda\ge100\sqrt{1+t^2}$, $1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda\le C$ for $|k|\le t$, and $t^{N+d/2}\lambda^{-\beta}\le Ct^{-\beta}$. Substituting step 5.1 in step 6.1 therefore gives $\mathcal Q\le C[\delta e^{D t^A}+t^{-\beta}]$ for a fixed $D>0$, after absorbing the polynomial factor $t^{d/2}\lambda^2$ into the exponential. For sufficiently small $0<\delta<t_0$, take $t=(\log(1/\delta)/(2D))^{1/A}\ge1$. The first term becomes $\sqrt\delta$, and the second is $C[\log(1/\delta)]^{-\beta/A}$. The former is bounded by a constant times the latter, since $e^{-x/2}x^{\beta/A}$ is bounded for $x\ge1$. Hence $\mathcal Q\le C[\log(1/\delta)]^{-\rho}$ with $\rho=\beta/A>0$. If $\delta=0$, let $t\to\infty$ in the estimate before this choice to obtain $\mathcal Q=0$.

Put $w=\log g_1-\log g_2$ and $H=g_1g_2$. Both $w$ and $
abla w$ have compact support in $\overline{\Omega'}$, and $w\in H_0^1(B)$. Expanding the formula for $Q$ gives the distribution identity $HQ=\operatorname{div}(H
abla w)$: the divergence part is $\Delta w$, while the zero-order part is $
abla\log H\cdot
abla w$. Test this identity with $w$ to obtain $\int H|
abla w|^2=-\langle Q,Hwangle$. The test is legitimate by $H^1$ approximation, since $Q$ is an $L^2$ field plus a divergence of an $L^2$ field and $Hw\in H_0^1(B)$. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle Q,Hwangle|\le\mathcal Q\|Hw\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^d)}\le C\mathcal Q\|w\|_{H^1(B)}$. Since $H\ge m_*>0$, Poincaré in [F5] implies $\|w\|_{H^1(B)}\le C\mathcal Q$; if this norm is zero the estimate is immediate, otherwise divide the resulting quadratic inequality by it. Finally the mean value theorem on the bounded interval of possible $\log g_j$ gives $|\gamma_1-\gamma_2|=|e^{2\log g_1}-e^{2\log g_2}|\le2\max\{M,1\}|w|$. Thus $\|\gamma_1-\gamma_2\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C\mathcal Q$. In particular $\delta=0$ forces equality of the coefficients.

Assume Countable Choice. Identify $\mathbb C$ with $\mathbb R^2$, use angular-frequency unitary Fourier transformation, and put $\partial=(\partial_x-i\partial_y)/2$, $\bar\partial=(\partial_x+i\partial_y)/2$. The Beurling transform $\mathcal B$ defined on $L^2(\mathbb C)$ by
$$\widehat{\mathcal Bf}(\xi)=\frac{\xi_1-i\xi_2}{\xi_1+i\xi_2}\widehat f(\xi)\qquad(\xi\ne0)$$
is an isometry and extends boundedly to every $L^p$, $1<p<\infty$. It commutes with translations. There is a finite constant $A\ge1$ such that, for $2\le p\le4$,
$$\|\mathcal B\|_{L^p\to L^p}\le A^{2-4/p}.$$
For $p>2$ and $f\in L^p$ supported in a fixed disk $D_R$, the absolutely convergent integral
$$\mathcal Cf(z):=\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{f(w)}{z-w}\,dA(w)$$
belongs to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb C)$, satisfies $\bar\partial\mathcal Cf=f$, $\partial\mathcal Cf=\mathcal Bf$, and obeys
$$\|\mathcal Cf\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_{p,R}\|f\|_p,\qquad |\mathcal Cf(z)-\mathcal Cf(z')|\le C_p\|f\|_p|z-z'|^{1-2/p}.$$
It is $O(1/|z|)$ at infinity. For every $0\le\kappa<1$ there is $p_\kappa>2$ such that, whenever $2\le p\le p_\kappa$ and $\mu,\nu$ are measurable with $\||\mu|+|\nu|\|_\infty\le\kappa$, the real-linear map
$$I-\mu\mathcal B-\nu\overline{\mathcal B},\qquad \overline{\mathcal B}(f):=\overline{\mathcal Bf},$$
is invertible on $L^p(\mathbb C;\mathbb C)$, with inverse norm at most $2/(1-\kappa)$.

([[thm-plancherel]], [[thm-complex-finite-simple-and-smooth-compact-support-density-for-finite-p]], [[thm-complex-lp-completeness-and-almost-everywhere-subsequences]])

proof_rows.text: For $f\in C_c^\infty$, [F1] shows that $Sf:=\partial\mathcal Cf$ is bounded locally and decays as $O(|z|^{-2})$, hence is in $L^2$. Distributional commutation gives $\bar\partial Sf=\partial f$. Fourier transformation gives $(i\xi_1-\xi_2)\widehat{Sf}=(i\xi_1+\xi_2)\widehat f$, so almost everywhere off the origin $\widehat{Sf}=((\xi_1-i\xi_2)/(\xi_1+i\xi_2))\widehat f$. The multiplier has modulus one. [F2] extends $S$ uniquely to the isometry $\mathcal B$ on $L^2$. Multiplication by the translation character commutes with this multiplier, giving translation commutation there.

The kernel $K(z)=-1/(\pi z^2)$ has annular integral $2\log2$. Its gradient is bounded by $C|z|^{-3}$, so for $|z|\ge2|h|$, the segment estimate gives $|K(z-h)-K(z)|\le C|h||z|^{-3}$. Polar integration from $2|h|$ to infinity bounds its integral by an absolute constant. The off-support representation for compactly supported $L^2$ inputs follows by approximating them by smooth inputs in one fixed compact neighborhood of their support: on any compact set at positive distance from that neighborhood the kernel integrals converge uniformly by Cauchy–Schwarz, while the operator outputs converge in $L^2$ by step 1.1. Exhausting the complement of the essential support by compact sets and shrinking the neighborhoods gives the representation almost everywhere off the essential support. Thus [F3] applies. Let $A=\max\{1,\|\mathcal B\|_{4\to4}\}$. Interpolating the norm-one $L^2$ bound and the $L^4$ bound gives $\|\mathcal B\|_{p\to p}\le A^\theta$ with $1/p=(1-\theta)/2+\theta/4$, that is $\theta=2-4/p$. Density makes all extensions compatible and carries translation commutation to every finite $p$.

Let $p>2$, let $q=p/(p-1)<2$, and let $f$ have support in $D_R$. Hölder gives absolute convergence of $\mathcal Cf$ at every $z$: the singularity $|z-w|^{-q}$ is locally integrable, and the support is bounded. For $\delta=|z-z'|>0$, split its kernel difference into the union of the two disks of radius $2\delta$ about $z,z'$ and its complement. On the first region, integrating the two singularities with Hölder bounds their contributions by $C_p\|f\|_p\delta^{1-2/p}$. On the complement, $|(z-w)^{-1}-(z'-w)^{-1}|\le C\delta|z-w|^{-2}$; its $L^q$ norm is at most $C_p\delta(\int_{2\delta}^\infty r^{1-2q}dr)^{1/q}=C_p\delta^{1-2/p}$. This proves the global Hölder bound. On $|z|\le2R$, the same singular-kernel estimate gives $|\mathcal Cf(z)|\le C_{p,R}\|f\|_p$; on $|z|>2R$, the bound is $C\|f\|_1/|z|\le C_R\|f\|_p/|z|$. The latter is $L^p$ because $p>2$, proving $\|\mathcal Cf\|_p\le C_{p,R}\|f\|_p$ and the stated decay. Approximate $f$ in $L^p$ by smooth functions supported in $D_{R+1}$. Their Cauchy transforms converge in $L^p$, and their two weak derivatives converge to $f$ and $\mathcal Bf$ by step 2.1. Passing the derivative identities against tests proves the two weak identities and the $W^{1,p}$ bound.

If $\kappa=0$, the final operator is the identity. Otherwise choose $2<p_\kappa\le4$ so close to $2$ that $\kappa A^{2-4/p_\kappa}\le(1+\kappa)/2<1$; this is possible by continuity and the value $1$ of the bound at $p=2$. For $2\le p\le p_\kappa$, the operator $Tf=\mu\mathcal Bf+\nu\overline{\mathcal Bf}$ has pointwise modulus at most $(|\mu|+|\nu|)|\mathcal Bf|$, and therefore norm at most $(1+\kappa)/2$. Regard $L^p(\mathbb C;\mathbb C)$ as a real Banach space. Its norm is at most $1/(1-(1+\kappa)/2)=2/(1-\kappa)$, proving the assertion.

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix $0\le\kappa<1$ and $R,S>0$. For every measurable $\mu$ supported in $D_R=\{|z|<R\}$ with $\|\mu\|_\infty\le\kappa$, there is a unique quasiconformal homeomorphism $\Phi:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ satisfying
$$\bar\partial\Phi=\mu\partial\Phi,\qquad \Phi(z)=z+O(1/z)\quad(z\to\infty).$$
Choose any fixed $2<r\le p_\kappa$ from the near-two inversion result, and put $\sigma=r-2>0$. Uniformly over all these coefficients,
$$\|\Phi-z\|_{W^{1,r}(\mathbb C)}+\|\Phi-z\|_\infty+[\Phi-z]_{C^{0,1-2/r}}\le C_{\kappa,r,R},\qquad \int_{D_S}|\partial\Phi|^{-\sigma}\,dA\le C_{\kappa,r,R,S}.$$
The Jacobian and $\partial\Phi$ are positive and nonzero almost everywhere, respectively, so the negative power is well-defined almost everywhere. In particular, for any $|k|=1$ and $f(z)=e^{ik\Phi(z)}$,
$$\|f\|_{W^{1,r}(D_S)}+\bigl\||\partial f|^{-1}\bigr\|_{L^\sigma(D_S)}\le C_{\kappa,r,R,S}.$$
For $0<\sigma<1$ the displayed $L^\sigma$ quantity means $(\int|\partial f|^{-\sigma})^{1/\sigma}$, without asserting a norm triangle inequality.

proof_rows.text: Take a solution from [F1] fixing infinity. Outside $D_R$ its coefficient is zero, so it is conformal there. In the infinity chart it is an injective holomorphic map fixing zero with nonzero derivative. Its Taylor expansion there gives $az+b+O(1/z)$ in the original chart, with $a\ne0$. Postcomposition by $(w-b)/a$ gives the principal normalization. Any two principal solutions differ by a Möbius map by [F1]; since both fix infinity this map is affine, and their leading and constant Laurent coefficients force it to be the identity. This proves existence and uniqueness of $\Phi$.

Set $h=\bar\partial\Phi$, which is in $L^2$ and has support in $\overline D_R$ by local quasiconformal Sobolev regularity and the zero coefficient outside. The Cauchy integral for compact $L^2$ data is locally $L^2$: on a fixed target disk the kernel restricted to all differences with $D_R$ is in $L^1$, so [F4] applies; outside a larger disk its bound is $C\|h\|_1/|z|$. Approximating $h$ by smooth functions in a fixed support disk yields distributionally $\bar\partial\mathcal Ch=h$ and $\partial\mathcal Ch=\mathcal Bh$, the latter by Beurling $L^2$ boundedness. Thus $\bar\partial(\Phi-z-\mathcal Ch)=0$. Applying $\partial$ and [F4] makes this distribution smooth harmonic; the original Cauchy–Riemann equation makes its representative holomorphic. It tends to zero at infinity by the principal normalization and the exterior Cauchy bound. Liouville gives $\Phi-z=\mathcal Ch$. Therefore $\partial\Phi=1+\mathcal Bh$, and the Beltrami equation says $(I-\mu\mathcal B)h=\mu$.

Let $h_r=(I-\mu\mathcal B)^{-1}\mu$ in $L^r$. Its norm is at most $C_\kappa\|\mu\|_r\le C_{\kappa,R,r}$ by [F3]. The equation gives $h_r=0$ outside $D_R$, hence $h_r\in L^2$ by Hölder on that disk. Compatibility of the $L^2$ and $L^r$ Beurling actions and uniqueness of the $L^2$ inverse imply $h_r=h$ from step 2.1. Apply the Cauchy bounds in [F3] to $\Phi-z=\mathcal Ch$. This proves its $W^{1,r}$, supremum and Hölder bounds. In particular $\Phi(D_S)$ lies in a disk of radius $S+C_{\kappa,R,r}$, uniformly in $\mu$.

By [F2], $\Psi=\Phi^{-1}$ has coefficient bounded by $\kappa$, supported in $\Phi(\overline D_R)$, and has the same principal expansion at infinity. Step 3.1 puts that support inside a fixed disk; applying step 3.1 to $\Psi$ therefore gives a uniform $L^r$ bound for $\partial\Psi$ on every fixed disk. At common differentiability points, the derivative inverse formula gives $|\partial\Psi(\Phi(z))|=1/[(1-|\mu(z)|^2)|\partial\Phi(z)|]$. Thus $|\partial\Phi(z)|^{-\sigma}\le|\partial\Psi(\Phi(z))|^\sigma$. Change variables with $z=\Psi(w)$ using [F2]; the bound $J_\Psi\le|\partial\Psi|^2$ gives $\int_{D_S}|\partial\Phi|^{-\sigma}\le\int_{\Phi(D_S)}|\partial\Psi(w)|^{\sigma+2}dA(w)$. Since $\sigma+2=r$, step 3.1 and the uniform disk containing $\Phi(D_S)$ bound the right side. Null-set preservation in [F2] justifies all inverse identities and negative powers on common full-measure sets.

On $D_S$, $|\Phi|\le S+C_{\kappa,R,r}$. For $|k|=1$, the exponential and its derivative therefore have bounded modulus above and away from zero. Smooth composition, first for smooth approximations on this bounded range and then by Sobolev convergence, gives $\partial f=ik e^{ik\Phi}\partial\Phi$ and the corresponding $\bar\partial$ formula. Step 3.1 supplies the $W^{1,r}$ bound, while $|\partial f|^{-\sigma}\le e^{\sigma(S+C)}|\partial\Phi|^{-\sigma}$ and step 4.1 supply the negative-power bound. This proves the final assertion, including the case $\sigma<1$ with its stated integral convention.

$$\int_{D_1}|\partial f_2|^{-\sigma}\,dA\le V^\sigma.$$
Then there is $C=C(\kappa,r,\theta,A,U,V,\sigma)$ such that, if $\varepsilon=\|f_1-f_2\|_{L^\infty(D_2)}\le1$,
$$\|\mu_1-\mu_2\|_{L^2(D_1)}\le C\varepsilon^\eta,\qquad \eta=\frac{\theta\sigma}{(1+\theta)(2+\sigma)}>0.$$

Therefore $|\bar\partial g|\le\kappa|\partial g|+|\alpha||g|$, so step 2.1 implies $g=0$. By [F3], $I-K$ is invertible. The equation $\eta-K\eta=\mathcal C(I-\nu\overline{\mathcal B})^{-1}\alpha=K\mathbf1_{D_1}$ has a unique $L^r$ solution. The equation itself and [F1] put $\eta\in W^{1,r}$, continuous with $O(1/z)$ decay. Reversing the ansatz calculation proves existence of $f_\mu$ and the asserted normalization. For any other solution, density of compact smooth functions in global $W^{1,r}$ gives $\partial\eta=\mathcal B\bar\partial\eta$; applying the inverse in [F1] and then $\mathcal C$ recovers the same integral equation, since its holomorphic residual vanishes at infinity. It therefore gives the same $\eta$. When $k=0$, $\alpha=0$, so $\eta=0$ and $f_\mu=1$.

Write $M=1+\eta$ from step 4.1. Its equation is $ ar\partial M=
u\overline{\partial M}+\alpha\overline M$, so $| ar\partial M|\le\kappa|\partial M|+|\alpha||M|$. Step 2.1 gives $M=e^a$, where $a=\mathcal Ch$ for data $h$ supported in $\overline D_1$ with $\|h\|_r\le C_{\kappa,r}\|\alpha\|_r\le C_{\kappa,r}|k|$. Thus $M$ never vanishes and $\|a\|_\infty+\|a\|_{W^{1,r}}\le C_{\kappa,r}|k|$. The bounds $|e^a-1|\le e^{\|a\|_\infty}|a|$ and $|
abla e^a|\le e^{\|a\|_\infty}|
abla a|$ prove the quantitative bound on $M-1$. The same Cauchy integral gives $|a(z)|\le C_{\kappa,r}|k|/|z|$ for $|z|>2$.

If $k\ne0$, set $\Phi=z+a/(ik)$. Then $f=e^{ik\Phi}$, $\Phi=z+O(1/z)$ and the asserted uniform deformation estimates follow from step 5.1. Since the exponential has no zeros, the chain rule in the Beltrami equation for $f$ gives $|\bar\partial\Phi|\le\kappa|\partial\Phi|$, with $\bar\partial\Phi=0$ outside $\overline D_1$. Define its complex coefficient by $\bar\partial\Phi/\partial\Phi$, using zero where both vanish, and take the principal homeomorphic solution $\Psi$ for that coefficient from [F2]. Step 1.1 gives $\Phi=H\circ\Psi$ with $H$ entire holomorphic. Both maps have the principal expansion, so $H(w)-w\to0$ at infinity. Liouville in [F4] gives $H(w)=w$, hence $\Phi=\Psi$ is a principal quasiconformal homeomorphism. Multiplication and composition with the exponential on $D_S$ now give the stated solution $W^{1,r}$ bound, while for $|k|=1$ the last clause of [F2] gives the inverse-gradient estimate. This completes all claims.

items.title: Positive power translation moduli after principal quasiconformal composition

references.title: Faraco and Prats, Characterization for stability in planar conductivities
references.locator: Section 4.3, Lemma 4.10 and its proof, printed pp. 23–25; the power-modulus specialization here uses mollification and the locally proved near-two Jacobian integrability.

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix $0\le\kappa<1$, $2<r\le p_\kappa$, $q\ge1$, and $L,R,A,B>0$. Put $p=qr/(r-2)$ and $\theta_0=1-2/r$. Let $\Phi$ be a principal quasiconformal homeomorphism with coefficient supported in $D_L$ and bounded by $\kappa$, and let $\Psi=\Phi^{-1}$. Suppose $v$ is measurable, supported in $D_R$, with $\|v\|_\infty\le B$ and
$$\omega_p(v,t):=\sup_{|h|\le t}\|v(\cdot-h)-v\|_p\le At^\theta\qquad(0<t\le1),$$
where $0<\theta\le1$. Then $v\circ\Psi$ is a well-defined almost-everywhere class, is supported in a fixed disk depending only on the listed parameters, and
$$\omega_q(v\circ\Psi,t)\le C t^{\theta\theta_0/(1+\theta)}\qquad(0<t\le1).$$
The constant is uniform over all such $v,\Phi$. Thus the positive power translation moduli furnished by bounded BV conductivities remain positive power moduli after these changes of variables.
items.facts:
**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice and the parameters and functions in the statement.

[F1] The principal maps $\Phi,\Psi$ have uniform bounded deformations and $C^{0,\theta_0}$ deformation seminorms; their derivatives are uniformly $L^r$ on fixed disks. Their Jacobians are positive almost everywhere, and both maps preserve null sets and satisfy the weighted area formula. ([[lem-ip-planar-principal-beltrami-inverse-gradient-integrability]], [[lem-inverse-of-a-quasiconformal-map-is-quasiconformal]], [[lem-analytic-quasiconformality-implies-modulus-distortion]])

[F2] Hölder applies with conjugate exponents $a=r/2>1$ and $a'=r/(r-2)$, and to the probability integral defining a nonnegative unit-mass mollification. ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are used in the quoted quasiconformal and integration interfaces. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

proof_rows.text: Choose a fixed nonnegative smooth unit-mass mollifier supported in the unit disk and let $v_h=\rho_h*v$, $0<h\le1$. The probability form of Hölder, followed by integration, gives $\|v-v_h\|_p\le\omega_p(v,h)\le Ah^\theta$. Also $\|v_h\|_\infty\le B$, $\|\nabla v_h\|_\infty\le C_\rho B/h$, and its support is contained in $\overline D_{R+1}$. The latter derivative bound follows by differentiating the smooth convolution kernel and taking its derivative's $L^1$ norm. All supports involved in $v_h\circ\Psi$ and $v\circ\Psi$ lie in $\Phi(\overline D_{R+1})$, hence inside one fixed disk by [F1]. Null-set preservation of $\Phi$ makes composition with $\Psi$ independent of the representative of $v$.

Apply the weighted area formula with $w=\Phi(z)$ and then Hölder. Since $J_\Phi\le|\partial\Phi|^2$, its $L^a$ norm on $D_{R+1}$ is uniformly bounded by [F1]. Thus $\|(v-v_h)\circ\Psi\|_q^q=\int|v-v_h|^qJ_\Phi\,dA\le\|v-v_h\|_{qa'}^q\|J_\Phi\|_{a}\le C A^qh^{q\theta}$, using $qa'=p$. Therefore the translation difference of this error has $L^q$ norm at most $2CAh^\theta$, by translation invariance of Lebesgue measure.

For $|y|\le t\le1$, the inverse deformation estimate gives $|\Psi(w-y)-\Psi(w)|\le|y|+C|y|^{\theta_0}\le C t^{\theta_0}$. The Lipschitz bound for $v_h$ therefore bounds $|v_h(\Psi(w-y))-v_h(\Psi(w))|$ by $CBh^{-1}t^{\theta_0}$. The support of this difference lies in the fixed disk from step 1.1 enlarged by one, whose area is uniformly bounded. Its $L^q$ norm is consequently at most $CBh^{-1}t^{\theta_0}$. Combine with step 2.1 and take $h=t^{\theta_0/(1+\theta)}$, which lies in $(0,1]$. The two powers $h^\theta$ and $h^{-1}t^{\theta_0}$ coincide with $t^{\theta\theta_0/(1+\theta)}$. Taking the supremum over the shifts proves the estimate.

items.title: Power decay for oscillatory complex-linear Beltrami phases

references.title: Faraco and Prats, Characterization for stability in planar conductivities
references.locator: Section 4.2, Proposition 4.4, Lemmas 4.5–4.6 and their complete proofs, printed pp. 16–23. For power moduli the proof here uses an L2 estimate on a smoothed truncated Cauchy kernel.

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix $0<\kappa<1$, $R,A>0$, $q>2$ and $0<\theta\le1$. Let $\mu$ be measurable, supported in $D_R$, with $\|\mu\|_\infty\le\kappa$ and $\omega_q(\mu,t)\le At^\theta$ for $0<t\le1$. For $v\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$ and $|c_v|=1$, let $\Psi_v$ be the principal quasiconformal solution of
$$\bar\partial\Psi_v(z)=c_v e^{iv\cdot z}\mu(z)\partial\Psi_v(z).$$
There exist $C>0$ and $b>0$, depending only on $\kappa,R,A,q,\theta$, such that
$$\sup_{z\in\mathbb C}|\Psi_v(z)-z|\le C|v|^{-b}\qquad(|v|\ge1).$$
Both constants are uniform in $\mu$, the direction of $v$ and its unimodular factor $c_v$.
items.facts:
**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice and the coefficient and parameters in the statement.

[F1] The Beurling transform has norm $1$ on $L^2$, is bounded on every strict $L^p$, and commutes with translations. One can choose $r>2$ so that $c:=\kappa\|\mathcal B\|_{r\to r}<1$. The Cauchy transform and near-two inverse identify the principal solution as $\Psi_v-z=\mathcal Ch_v$, where $h_v=(I-c_ve^{iv\cdot z}\mu\mathcal B)^{-1}(c_ve^{iv\cdot z}\mu)$ is supported in $\overline D_R$. ([[lem-ip-planar-cauchy-beurling-and-near-two-inversion]], [[lem-ip-planar-principal-beltrami-inverse-gradient-integrability]])

[F2] Plancherel and Fourier inversion hold; convolution becomes a Fourier product. Young's convolution inequality holds, including $L^{r'}*L^r\to L^\infty$. ([[thm-plancherel]], [[thm-fourier-transform-converts-convolution-to-products]], [[thm-l-one-fourier-inversion]], [[thm-young-convolution-inequality]])

[F3] A holomorphic function on an exterior disk, continuous to its boundary and tending to zero at infinity, has supremum bounded by its boundary supremum. ([[thm-maximum-modulus-principle-with-boundary-and-infinity-control]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are used at [F1]–[F3]. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

proof_rows.text:
Write $K=|v|$, $
u=c_ve^{iv\cdot z}\mu$, and $h_n=(
u\mathcal B)^n
u$. The Neumann series $h_v=\sum_{n\ge0}h_n$ converges in $L^r$ by [F1]. For $g_N=\sum_{n=0}^Nh_n$ and $b_N=h_v-g_N$, one has $\|b_N\|_r\le Cc^{N+1}$ and $\|g_N\|_r\le C$. Also $\|g_N\|_2\le C$, because $\|
u\mathcal B\|_{2	o2}\le\kappa<1$. All these functions have support in $\overline D_R$. Define $f_n=c_v^{-(n+1)}e^{-i(n+1)v\cdot z}h_n$. Then $f_0=\mu$ and $f_n=\mu T_nf_{n-1}$, where $T_nu=e^{-inv\cdot z}\mathcal B(e^{inv\cdot z}u)$. This is a translation-invariant Fourier multiplier, and $\|T_n\|_{p	o p}=\|\mathcal B\|_{p	o p}$, since the two modulation factors have modulus one.

Put $\ell=2q/(q-2)$, so $1/2=1/q+1/\ell$, and $M=2+\|\mathcal B\|_{\ell\to\ell}$. Iteration of the product norm gives $\|f_n\|_\ell\le C_R\kappa^{n+1}\|\mathcal B\|_{\ell\to\ell}^n$. The translation product identity and Hölder give $\omega_2(f_n,t)\le\omega_q(\mu,t)\|T_nf_{n-1}\|_\ell+\kappa\omega_2(T_nf_{n-1},t)$. By translation commutation and the $L^2$ norm one, the second term is at most $\kappa\omega_2(f_{n-1},t)$. For $n=0$, bounded support gives $\omega_2(f_0,t)\le C_R\omega_q(\mu,t)$. Induction therefore yields $\omega_2(f_n,t)\le C_RA\kappa^nM^nt^\theta$ for $0<t\le1$: the two induction contributions are bounded by $M^{n-1}$ and $\|\mathcal B\|_{\ell\to\ell}^n$, whose sum is at most $M^n$ after increasing the fixed constant.

For any $L^2$ function $f$ and $T>0$, averaging $\|f(\cdot-y)-f\|_2^2$ over $[-2/T,2/T]^2$ and using Plancherel gives the multiplier $2[1-\operatorname{sinc}(2\xi_1/T)\operatorname{sinc}(2\xi_2/T)]$. On $|\xi|\ge T$, one sinc factor has absolute value at most $1/\sqrt2$; the multiplier is bounded below by a positive absolute constant. Hence $\|\mathbf1_{\{|\xi|\ge T\}}\widehat f\|_2\le C\omega_2(f,3/T)$. Since $\widehat h_n$ is the shifted transform of $f_n$ by $(n+1)v$, the disk $|\xi|\le K/2$ samples $\widehat f_n$ only at frequencies at least $K/2$. Step 2.1 therefore gives, when $K\ge6$, $\|\widehat g_N\|_{L^2(D_{K/2})}\le C A M^{N+1}K^{-\theta}$, by summing the geometric upper bounds and discarding the beneficial factors $\kappa^n$.

Fix a smooth compactly supported cutoff kernel $P(z)$ equal to $1/(\pi z)$ on $|z|<2R+1$. On $D_R$, convolution $P*h_v$ equals $\mathcal Ch_v$. The latter is holomorphic outside $\overline D_R$, continuous everywhere and tends to zero at infinity, so [F3] shows that a supremum estimate on $D_R$ controls its global supremum. Let $r'=r/(r-1)\in(1,2)$, $\theta_0=1-2/r>0$, and $P_\delta=\rho_\delta*P$ for a fixed smooth nonnegative mollifier. Then $\|P-P_\delta\|_{r'}\le C\delta^{\theta_0}$, $\|P_\delta\|_2\le C\delta^{-1}$, and $\|\nabla P_\delta\|_2\le C\delta^{-2}$. For the first assertion, split a translation difference of $P$ into disks of radius $3|y|$ at its two singularities and their complement. Hölder integration of $|z|^{-r'}$ on the disks gives the power $|y|^{2/r'-1}$; off them use the derivative bound $C|y||z|^{-2}$ and integrate its $r'$-power from $|y|$ to the fixed cutoff radius, giving the same power. Integrating this estimate against $\rho_\delta(y)$ proves the first bound. The other two follow from Young applied to $P\in L^1$ and the scaled $L^2$ norms of $\rho_\delta$ and its derivative.

The tail $P*b_N$ has supremum at most $C\|b_N\|_r\le Cc^{N+1}$, and $(P-P_\delta)*g_N$ has supremum at most $C\delta^{\theta_0}$, by step 4.1 and the $L^r$ bounds of step 1.1. Fourier inversion and Cauchy–Schwarz bound the remaining term by $C\|\widehat P_\delta\widehat g_N\|_1$. Below frequency $K/2$, steps 3.1–4.1 bound it by $C\delta^{-1} A M^{N+1}K^{-\theta}$. Above that frequency, Plancherel gives $\|\widehat P_\delta\|_{L^2(\{|\xi|>K/2\})}\le CK^{-1}\|\nabla P_\delta\|_2\le CK^{-1}\delta^{-2}$; combine this with $\|g_N\|_2\le C$. We have proved $\|\Psi_v-z\|_\infty\le C[c^N+\delta^{\theta_0}+\delta^{-1}M^{N+1}K^{-\theta}+K^{-1}\delta^{-2}]$.

Choose $a=\theta/(4\log M)$, $N=\lfloor a\log K\rfloor$ and $\delta=K^{-\theta/4}$. For sufficiently large $K$, $c^N\le C K^{a\log c}$, $M^{N+1}\le M K^{\theta/4}$, and the four terms in step 5.1 are bounded by $C K^{-b}$ with $b=\min\{-a\log c,\theta\theta_0/4,\theta/2,1/2\}>0$. Indeed, the third term has exponent at most $-\theta/2$ and the fourth at most $-1/2$ because $\theta\le1$. The remaining bounded interval of $1\le K$ is absorbed by increasing $C$, using the uniform principal deformation bound in [F1]. This proves the result uniformly in all stated parameters and phase directions.

items.title: Uniform power phase decay for Beltrami CGO solutions

references.title: Faraco and Prats, Characterization for stability in planar conductivities
references.locator: Section 4.3, Theorem 4.13 and complete inverse-phase argument, printed pp. 25–27.

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix $0<\kappa<1$, choose $2<r\le p_\kappa$, and put $p=4r/(r-2)$. Suppose $\mu\in L^\infty(\mathbb C;\mathbb C)$ is supported in $D_1$, $\|\mu\|_\infty\le\kappa$, and $\omega_p(\mu,t)\le At^\theta$ for $0<t\le1$, with fixed $A>0$ and $0<\theta\le1$. Let $f_\mu(z,k)=e^{ik\Phi_\mu(z,k)}$ be its measurable-coefficient Beltrami CGO solution and principal phase. There exist constants $C,b>0$, depending only on $\kappa,r,A,\theta$, such that
$$|\Phi_\mu(z,k)-z|\le C\min\{(1+|z|)^{-1},|k|^{-b}\}\qquad(z\in\mathbb C,\ |k|\ge1).$$
The same constants apply to every coefficient $\lambda\mu$, $|\lambda|=1$.
items.facts:
**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice and the data in the statement.

[F1] The CGO phase $\Phi$ is a principal quasiconformal homeomorphism, conformal outside $\overline D_1$, with uniform deformation bounds and $|\Phi(z)-z|\le C/(1+|z|)$. Its inverse has the same dilatation and the standard inverse derivative identity. ([[lem-ip-planar-measurable-beltrami-cgo-solutions]], [[lem-ip-planar-principal-beltrami-inverse-gradient-integrability]], [[lem-inverse-of-a-quasiconformal-map-is-quasiconformal]])

[F2] If $p=4r/(r-2)$ and $\omega_p(\mu,t)\le At^\theta$, then composition with the inverse of any principal phase in [F1] gives a uniformly bounded-support coefficient with $L^4$ translation modulus at most $Ct^{\theta'}$, where $\theta'=\theta(1-2/r)/(1+\theta)>0$. ([[lem-ip-planar-qc-composition-preserves-power-translation-moduli]])

[F3] A principal solution of $\bar\partial\Psi=c e^{iv\cdot w}\widetilde\mu\partial\Psi$, with $|c|=1$, $|\widetilde\mu|\le\kappa$, fixed bounded support and uniform positive power $L^4$ translation modulus, has $\|\Psi-w\|_\infty\le C|v|^{-b}$ for some uniform $b>0$. ([[lem-ip-planar-oscillatory-beltrami-phase-decay]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are used at [F1]–[F3]. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

proof_rows.text: Write $\Phi=\Phi_\mu(\cdot,k)$ and $\Psi=\Phi^{-1}$. The equation $\bar\partial f=\mu\overline{\partial f}$ with $f=e^{ik\Phi}$ gives $\bar\partial\Phi=-(\overline k/k)\mu e^{-i(k\Phi+\overline k\overline\Phi)}\overline{\partial\Phi}$. The nonvanishing exponential permits division, and all derivatives agree almost everywhere by [F1]. Apply the inverse derivative identity: its two derivative factors cancel the quotient $\overline{\partial\Phi}/\partial\Phi$, leaving $\bar\partial\Psi(w)=(\overline k/k)e^{-i(kw+\overline k\overline w)}\mu(\Psi(w))\partial\Psi(w)$. Thus this is a complex-linear Beltrami equation with oscillation vector of length $2|k|$ and coefficient $\widetilde\mu=\mu\circ\Psi$. Its support lies in the fixed disk containing $\Phi(D_1)$ by [F1].

By [F2], $\widetilde\mu$ has uniform positive power $L^4$ translation modulus; its supremum bound remains $\kappa$, with almost-everywhere composition justified by null-set preservation in [F1]. It is legitimate that $\widetilde\mu$ depends on $k$, because [F3] is uniform over the entire coefficient family with these support and modulus bounds. Apply [F3] to the equation in step 1.1 to obtain $\|\Psi-w\|_\infty\le C|k|^{-b}$. Since $\Phi$ is onto, $|\Phi(z)-z|=|\Phi(z)-\Psi(\Phi(z))|\le C|k|^{-b}$. Combine this with the spatial decay in [F1] to obtain the stated minimum bound. Multiplication of $\mu$ by a unimodular constant preserves every support, supremum and translation-modulus hypothesis; the constants therefore work for all $\lambda\mu$.

items.title: Conductivity CGO solutions and continuous logarithmic phases

references.title: Astala and Päivärinta, Calderón's inverse conductivity problem in the plane
references.locator: Section 4, Proposition 4.3 and full proof, printed pp. 279–280; Section 1, equations (1.14)–(1.17).

references.title: Faraco and Prats, Characterization for stability in planar conductivities
references.locator: Section 4.4, Lemmas 4.14 and 4.18 and Proposition 4.19 with proofs, printed pp. 27–30.

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\mu$ be real, supported in $D_1$ and bounded by $0<\kappa<1$, and put $\gamma=(1-\mu)/(1+\mu)$. Let $f_\pm=f_{\pm\mu}$ be the measurable Beltrami CGO solutions. Then
$$\operatorname{Re}\frac{f_+(z,k)}{f_-(z,k)}>0,\qquad u_\gamma(z,k):=\operatorname{Re}f_+(z,k)+i\operatorname{Im}f_-(z,k)\ne0.$$
The function $u_\gamma$ solves $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla u_\gamma)=0$ weakly, has the form $e^{ikz}(1+R_\gamma)$ with $R_\gamma\in W^{1,r}(\mathbb C)$ and $R_\gamma(z,k)=O(1/z)$, and $u_\gamma(\cdot,0)=1$. For $k\ne0$ there is a continuous logarithmic phase $\delta_\gamma(\cdot,k)$, uniquely normalized by
$$u_\gamma(z,k)=e^{\delta_\gamma(z,k)},\qquad \delta_\gamma(z,k)-ikz=O(1/z)\quad(z\to\infty).$$
It maps $\mathbb C$ onto $\mathbb C$. If the power-modulus hypotheses of the Beltrami phase-decay result hold, uniformly for unimodular multiples of $\mu$, then for some $C,b>0$,
$$|\delta_\gamma(z,k)-ikz|\le C|k|\min\{(1+|z|)^{-1},|k|^{-b}\}\qquad(|k|\ge1).$$
For each fixed $k$, $u_\gamma$ is uniformly Hölder continuous on every fixed disk, with an exponent $1-2/r>0$ and a constant depending only on that disk, $\kappa,r,|k|$.
items.facts:
**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice and the real coefficient and parameters in the statement.

[F1] The normalized multipliers $M_{\pm\mu}$ never vanish and obey uniform $W^{1,r}$ and supremum bounds. The local similarity proof gives $F=c e^a$ whenever a bounded normalized function satisfies $|\bar\partial F|\le\kappa\mathbf1_{D_1}|\partial F|+B\mathbf1_{D_1}|F|$, with its limiting value $c$ at infinity. The CGO solution depends continuously on a unimodular coefficient rotation in $W^{1,r}$ and uniformly on compact sets, by the same Fredholm construction and its resolvent identity. ([[lem-ip-planar-measurable-beltrami-cgo-solutions]])

[F2] The principal phases for all rotated coefficients have uniform spatial decay and, under the extra modulus hypothesis, uniform power decay in $|k|$. The Cauchy transform has Hölder exponent $1-2/r$. ([[lem-ip-planar-beltrami-cgo-power-phase-decay]], [[lem-ip-planar-cauchy-beurling-and-near-two-inversion]])

[F3] The winding number of a loop in the punctured plane is its circle degree, is invariant under homotopy there, and vanishes for a null-homotopic loop. ([[thm-winding-number-equals-circle-degree]], [[cor-winding-number-classifies-loops-in-the-punctured-plane]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are inherited from these analytic interfaces. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

proof_rows.text: Put $M_\pm=e^{-ikz}f_\pm$. Their equations are $\bar\partial M_\pm=\pm\mu e^{-i(kz+\overline k\overline z)}(\overline{\partial M_\pm}-i\overline k\overline M_\pm)$. For every real $t$, the combination $G=M_+-itM_-$ satisfies the same displayed equation with its plus coefficient, because conjugation changes $-it$ to $it$. It therefore obeys the similarity inequality in [F1], with $B=|k|\kappa$, and tends to $1-it$ at infinity. Thus $G=(1-it)e^a$ and has no zeros. The continuous ratio $M_+/M_-$ tends to $1$ at infinity and never meets the imaginary axis: a value $it$ would give a zero of $G$. If its real part were nonpositive anywhere, continuity along a path to a sufficiently large point would force such an imaginary-axis value. Hence its real part is strictly positive everywhere. Since the exponential prefactors cancel, this is also the ratio $f_+/f_-$.

Write $f_+=a+ib$. The equation $\bar\partial f_+=\mu\overline{\partial f_+}$ with real $\mu$ gives $b_y=\gamma a_x$ and $b_x=-\gamma a_y$. Equality of the mixed weak derivatives of $b$ implies $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla a)=0$. The same computation for $f_-$, with coefficient $-\mu$, shows that its imaginary part solves the $\gamma$ equation. Thus their stated complex combination $u_\gamma$ solves that equation. Setting $A=f_++f_-$ and $B=f_+-f_-$ gives $u_\gamma=(A+\overline B)/2$. Step 1.1 is equivalent to $|B|<|A|$, so $u_\gamma\ne0$. Its normalized remainder is $R_\gamma=\tfrac12[M_++M_-+e^{-i(kz+\overline k\overline z)}(\overline M_+-\overline M_-)]-1$. The multiplier bounds in [F1] and differentiation of the unit-modulus exponential give $R_\gamma\in W^{1,r}$ and its $O(1/z)$ normalization; the case $k=0$ follows from $f_\pm=1$.

For every constant $|\lambda|=1$, uniqueness of the CGO solution gives $f_{\lambda\mu}=\tfrac12[(1+\lambda)f_++(1-\lambda)f_-]=(A+\lambda B)/2$. To check its equation, the constants $a=(1+\lambda)/2$, $b=(1-\lambda)/2$ satisfy $a=\lambda\overline a$ and $-b=\lambda\overline b$; substitution proves the required real-linear Beltrami equation, and $a+b=1$ gives the normalization. At a point where $B\ne0$, choose $\lambda(z,k)=\overline B/B$; where $B=0$, choose any unit value. Then $u_\gamma(z,k)=f_{\lambda(z,k)\mu}(z,k)$. Each right side is $e^{ik\Phi_{\lambda\mu}(z,k)}$.

For fixed $k\ne0$, the phases $\Phi_{\lambda\mu}$ depend continuously on $\lambda$ and $z$. Indeed, the coefficients in the Fredholm construction of [F1] depend continuously on $\lambda$ in operator norm; the resolvent identity gives continuity of its solution locally in $\lambda$, hence on the compact parameter circle. Its nonvanishing normalized multiplier admits the uniquely determined logarithm tending to zero at infinity. That logarithm depends continuously on $\lambda$ on compact sets: start at a uniformly large base point where all multipliers are close to $1$, use the principal logarithm there, and extend along a finite covering of any fixed compact path by disks where the multipliers stay away from zero. The resulting phase is the normalized principal phase in [F2]. Therefore $\widetilde\delta(z)=ik\Phi_{\lambda(z,k)\mu}(z,k)$ is continuous where $B\ne0$. If $B(z_0,k)=0$, all values $f_{\lambda\mu}(z_0,k)$ coincide. Their phases have equal exponentials and vary continuously with $\lambda$, so their differences belong to the discrete set $2\pi i\mathbb Z$ and are constant; they are thus all equal. Compactness of the rotation circle and joint continuity then give continuity of $\widetilde\delta$ also at $z_0$. Its exponential is $u_\gamma$ by step 3.1, and [F2] gives its required normalization and bounds. Uniqueness follows because any two continuous logarithms on the connected plane differ by a constant $2\pi i n$, which the normalization forces to be zero.

The phase $\delta_\gamma=\widetilde\delta$ differs from $ikz$ by a bounded function. For any target $w$, choose a large circle $|z|=R$ on which $|\delta_\gamma(z)-ikz|+|w|<|k|R$. The straight homotopy between $\delta_\gamma(z)-w$ and $ikz$ avoids zero on this circle, so their winding numbers are both one. If $\delta_\gamma-w$ had no zero in the disk, its boundary loop would extend to a loop through a disk in $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ and would have winding zero, a contradiction. Thus the phase is onto. Finally the Hölder and supremum bounds on $M_\pm$ in [F1]–[F2], combined with the smooth exponential on a fixed disk, give the asserted Hölder estimate for $f_\pm$ and hence for their real and imaginary combination $u_\gamma$.

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix $0\le\kappa<1$ and $2<r\le p_\kappa$. Let $\nu,\alpha,E$ be measurable and supported in $D_1$, with $\|\nu\|_\infty\le\kappa$, $\|\alpha\|_\infty\le B$ and $E\in L^r$. If $F\in W^{1,r}(\mathbb C)$ is continuous, tends to zero at infinity, and satisfies
$$\bar\partial F=\nu\overline{\partial F}+\alpha\overline F+E,$$
then
$$\|F\|_{W^{1,r}(\mathbb C)}+\|F\|_\infty\le C_{\kappa,r}e^{C_{\kappa,r}(1+B)}\|E\|_r.$$
The constants do not depend on the measurable coefficients or on the particular solution.
items.facts:
**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice and the functions and parameters in the statement.

[F1] The complex-linear equation $\bar\partial a-\eta\partial a=h$ with $|\eta|\le\kappa$ and both data supported in $D_1$ has the solution $a=\mathcal C(I-\eta\mathcal B)^{-1}h$, with $\|a\|_{W^{1,r}}+\|a\|_\infty\le C_{\kappa,r}\|h\|_r$ and $a\to0$ at infinity. ([[lem-ip-planar-cauchy-beurling-and-near-two-inversion]])

[F2] A continuous locally $H^1$ solution of $\bar\partial G=\eta\partial G$, with $|\eta|\le\kappa$ and compact support of $\eta$, factors through the principal quasiconformal coordinate as an entire holomorphic function; hence a bounded solution tending to zero is zero. This factorization is proved locally in the CGO construction. ([[lem-ip-planar-measurable-beltrami-cgo-solutions]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are used at [F1]–[F2]. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

proof_rows.text:
Define $a=
u\overline{\partial F}/\partial F$ where $\partial F
e0$ and $a=0$ otherwise, and define $b=\alpha\overline F/F$ where $F
e0$ and $b=0$ otherwise. Then $a,b$ are measurable, supported in $D_1$, satisfy $|a|\le\kappa$, $|b|\le B$, and the equation becomes $ ar\partial F=a\partial F+bF+E$. The identities also hold on the zero denominator sets, because the corresponding original terms are zero there. Let $s=\mathcal C(I-a\mathcal B)^{-1}b$. By [F1], $ ar\partial s-a\partial s=b$, $s	o0$ at infinity, and $\|s\|_{W^{1,r}}+\|s\|_\infty\le C B$.

Put $G=e^{-s}F$. The weak product and composition rules follow by local smooth approximation, since both factors are continuous and bounded on compact sets and their derivatives are in $L^r$. The equation in step 1.1 gives $\bar\partial G-a\partial G=e^{-s}E$. The particular solution $G_0=\mathcal C(I-a\mathcal B)^{-1}(e^{-s}E)$ obeys $\|G_0\|_{W^{1,r}}+\|G_0\|_\infty\le C e^{CB}\|E\|_r$, by [F1]. Both $G$ and $G_0$ are continuous and tend to zero at infinity; their difference is bounded and solves the homogeneous equation. By [F2], $G=G_0$. Finally $F=e^sG_0$, so the product rule gives $\|F\|_{W^{1,r}}+\|F\|_\infty\le C e^{CB}(1+\|\nabla s\|_r)(\|G_0\|_{W^{1,r}}+\|G_0\|_\infty)\le C e^{C(1+B)}\|E\|_r$. This proves the estimate.

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\mu$ be real, supported in $D_1$, and $\|\mu\|_\infty\le\kappa<1$. Fix $2<r\le p_\kappa$. Write $f_\pm=e^{ikz}M_\pm$, let $b_\pm(k)$ be the coefficients of $z^{-1}$ in the holomorphic exterior expansions $M_\pm(z,k)=1+b_\pm(k)/z+O(z^{-2})$, and define
$$\tau_\mu(k):=\tfrac12\overline{b_+(k)-b_-(k)}.$$
The functions $k\mapsto M_\pm(\cdot,k)-1$ are smooth into $W^{1,r}(\mathbb C)$ and
$$\|\nabla_k M_\pm(\cdot,k)\|_{W^{1,r}}+\|\nabla_k M_\pm(\cdot,k)\|_\infty+|\nabla_k\tau_\mu(k)|\le C_{\kappa,r}e^{C_{\kappa,r}(1+|k|)}.$$
The amplitude obeys $\tau_\mu(0)=0$ and $|\tau_\mu(k)|\le1$. The conductivity CGO solution and its normalized logarithmic phase satisfy
$$\bar\partial_k u_\gamma(z,k)=-i\tau_\mu(k)\overline{u_\gamma(z,k)},\qquad \bar\partial_k\delta_\gamma(z,k)=-i\tau_\mu(k)e^{\overline{\delta_\gamma(z,k)}-\delta_\gamma(z,k)}.$$
For every fixed $S>0$, $|\nabla_k\delta_\gamma(z,k)|\le C_{\kappa,r,S}e^{C_{\kappa,r,S}(1+|k|)}$ on $D_S$. The phase is normalized by $\delta_\gamma(z,0)=0$.
