**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice and the coefficient and exponent in the statement.

[F1] The real-linear Fredholm construction supplies unique normalized CGO solutions, continuous nonvanishing multipliers, uniform $W^{1,r}$ bounds and their principal phases. The Cauchy and near-two inverse bounds hold for compact data. ([[lem-ip-planar-measurable-beltrami-cgo-solutions]], [[lem-ip-planar-cauchy-beurling-and-near-two-inversion]])

[F2] A forced real-linear Beltrami solution with a bounded compact lower-order coefficient of size $B$ has $W^{1,r}$ and supremum norms at most $Ce^{C(1+B)}$ times the forcing norm. ([[lem-ip-planar-forced-beltrami-similarity-estimate]])

[F3] The conductivity combination never vanishes; $\operatorname{Re}(M_+/M_-)>0$, and its logarithmic phase has the principal spatial normalization. A unit-disk holomorphic self-map fixing zero has derivative at zero of modulus at most one. ([[lem-ip-planar-conductivity-cgo-logarithmic-phases]], [[thm-unit-disc-schwarz-lemma-with-rigidity]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are inherited from [F1]–[F3]. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

proof_rows.text: Put $e_k(z)=e^{i(kz+\overline k\overline z)}$, $A_k=\partial_z+ik$, and define the complex-antilinear operator $L_k g=\mathcal C[\mu e_{-k}\overline{A_k g}]$ on the real Banach space $Y=W^{1,r}(\mathbb C)\oplus\mathbb C$. It is bounded into $W^{1,r}$ and smooth in the two real coordinates of $k$, because its coefficient derivatives are bounded multiplications on the fixed disk. Both $I-L_k$ and $I+L_k$ are invertible on $Y$. To verify surjectivity rather than assume it, prescribe a right side $h+c\in Y$, put the desired unknown equal to $h+c+j$, and differentiate the equation for $j$. Its derivative equation is $(I-\mu e_{-k}\overline{\mathcal B})\bar\partial j=\alpha\overline j+E$, with $\alpha=-i\overline k\mu e_{-k}$ and compact forcing $E=\mu e_{-k}\overline{\partial h}+\alpha(\overline h+\overline c)$. It reduces to the same compact Fredholm operator as [F1], with arbitrary compact $L^r$ forcing, so gives a unique $j\in W^{1,r}$. Replacing $\mu$ by $-\mu$ proves the other sign. The bounded inverse follows from this Fredholm solution formula. Resolvent identities therefore imply that $M_\pm=(I\mp L_k)^{-1}1$ depend smoothly on $k$ in $Y$, with constant component always $1$.

Differentiating the multiplier equation with respect to either real coordinate of $k$ gives an equation for $W=\partial_{k_j}M_\pm$ with principal coefficient of modulus at most $\kappa$, lower-order coefficient bounded by $C|k|$, and compact forcing bounded in $L^r$ by $C(1+|k|)(1+\|M_\pm-1\|_{W^{1,r}})$. Coefficient derivatives contribute only bounded factors $z,\overline z$ on $D_1$. By [F1] this forcing is at most $Ce^{C(1+|k|)}$. The derivatives $W$ are continuous, in $W^{1,r}$, and tend to zero at infinity by the compact Cauchy representation and its differentiated data. Apply [F2] to get the claimed derivative bounds. The integral identity $\overline{b_\pm}=\pi^{-1}\int(\pm\mu)\partial_z(e_kM_\pm)\,dA$ follows by integrating the compact Cauchy data for $M_\pm-1$ and conjugating, using that $\mu$ is real. Differentiation under this compact integral, justified by the just-proved $W^{1,r}$ bounds, gives the stated derivative bound on $\tau$.

Define $F_+=(M_++M_-)/2$, $J=(M_+-M_-)/2$, and $F_-=i e_{-k}\overline J$. Adding and subtracting the multiplier equations gives $F_+=1+L_kJ$ and $J=L_kF_+$, hence $(I-L_k^2)F_+=1$. The square is complex-linear and $I-L_k^2=(I-L_k)(I+L_k)$ is invertible. Put $Q_k h=e_{-k}\overline{\mathcal C}(e_kh)$, where $\overline{\mathcal C}$ has kernel $1/(\pi(\overline z-\overline w))$. Direct kernel differentiation gives, for fixed compact data $h$, $\bar\partial_kQ_kh=-i e_{-k}\pi^{-1}\int e_kh\,dA$: the derivative of the exponential cancels the kernel denominator. Composing the two antilinear factors of $L_k$ gives $L_k^2g=\mathcal C\mu\bar\partial_zQ_k\mu A_kg$. Since $\bar\partial_k A_k=0$, it follows for fixed $g\in Y$ that $\bar\partial_k(L_k^2)g=-i t(g;k)\mathcal C(\mu\bar\partial_ze_{-k})$, where $t(g;k)=\pi^{-1}\int\mu\partial_z(e_kg)dA$. All these identities hold first for smooth compact data by the displayed integrals and then by $L^r$ approximation and boundedness of the composed operators.

The coefficient identity in step 2.1 gives $t(F_+;k)=\tfrac12(\overline b_+-\overline b_-)=\tau$. Also $J=L_k1+L_k^2J$ and $J=i e_{-k}\overline F_-$ imply $(I-L_k^2)(e_{-k}\overline F_-)=-i\mathcal C(\mu\bar\partial_ze_{-k})$. Differentiate $(I-L_k^2)F_+=1$ with respect to $\overline k$ and apply step 3.1 and complex linearity of the inverse. Uniqueness yields $\bar\partial_kF_+=\tau e_{-k}\overline F_-$. The definitions further give $F_+=1-i\mathcal C(\mu\bar\partial_zF_-)$ and $F_-=iQ_k\mu A_kF_+$. Differentiating the latter identity, using the rank-one formula of step 3.1 and the first derivative identity just proved, gives $\bar\partial_kF_-=\tau e_{-k}[1+i\overline{\mathcal C}(\mu\partial_z\overline F_-)]=\tau e_{-k}\overline F_+$. Since $u_\gamma=e^{ikz}(F_+-iF_-)$, these two identities give $\bar\partial_ku_\gamma=-i\tau\overline{u_\gamma}$. Division by the nonzero solution in [F3] gives the displayed phase equation.

By [F3], $|J/F_+|<1$. Outside $\overline D_1$ this quotient is holomorphic, and it tends to zero at infinity. Thus $w\mapsto J(1/w)/F_+(1/w)$ extends to a holomorphic disk self-map vanishing at zero. Its derivative there is $(b_+-b_-)/2$, so Schwarz's lemma in [F3] gives $|\tau|\le1$. At $k=0$, $M_+=M_-=1$, giving $\tau(0)=0$. For $z\in D_S$, the pointwise rotated-coefficient representation in [F3] and the uniform principal deformation bound in [F1] give $|u_\gamma(z,k)|\ge e^{-C_S|k|}$. Step 2.1 bounds $|\nabla_ku_\gamma|$ by $Ce^{C_S(1+|k|)}$. Dividing gives the asserted derivative bound for $\delta_\gamma$. The normalized multipliers tend to $1$ as $k\to0$ by [F1], so the phase continues smoothly there with value zero. This completes all claims.

references.title: Barceló, Faraco and Ruiz, Stability of Calderón inverse conductivity problem in the plane

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $0<a<1$, $0\le\kappa<1$, and let real $\mu_1,\mu_2$ be supported in $D_a$, with $\|\mu_j\|_\infty\le\kappa$. Set $\gamma_j=(1-\mu_j)/(1+\mu_j)$, and define their weak DN maps on $D_1$ and their scattering amplitudes $\tau_j$ by the preceding CGO construction. If $E=\mathcal D(D_1)/\mathbb C\mathbf1$ and
$$\delta=\|\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_2}\|_{\mathcal L(E,E^*)},$$
then
$$|\tau_1(k)-\tau_2(k)|\le C_\kappa\delta |k|e^{C_\kappa(1+|k|)}\qquad(k\in\mathbb C).$$
In particular this is at most $C_\kappa\delta e^{C_\kappa(1+|k|)}$ after increasing the constant; the assertion includes $k=0$.
items.facts:
**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice and the coefficients in the statement.

[F1] In the exterior disk, $u_j(z,k)=e^{ikz}A_j(z,k)+e^{-i\overline k\overline z}\overline{J_j(z,k)}$, where $A_j=(M_{+\mu_j}+M_{-\mu_j})/2=1+O(1/z)$ and $J_j=(M_{+\mu_j}-M_{-\mu_j})/2=\overline{\tau_j(k)}/z+O(z^{-2})$ are holomorphic. Moreover $\|u_j(\cdot,k)-1\|_{H^1(D_1)}\le C|k|e^{C(1+|k|)}$, by the uniform multiplier bounds. ([[lem-ip-planar-measurable-beltrami-cgo-solutions]], [[lem-ip-planar-conductivity-cgo-logarithmic-phases]], [[lem-ip-planar-scattering-dbar-equation-and-parameter-bounds]])

[F2] The weak DN maps are well-defined, Hermitian, kill constants, and their difference has the stated constant-quotient norm. ([[lem-ip-calderon-rough-dn-map-wellposedness]], [[lem-ip-calderon-rough-alessandrini-and-quotient-norm]])

[F3] A circle integral of a holomorphic Laurent expansion picks its $z^{-1}$ coefficient. Green's second identity applies to harmonic functions on a smooth annulus. ([[cor-residue-theorem-circle]], [[cor-second-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are inherited from the analytic and weak-solution interfaces. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

proof_rows.text: The disk weak-solution interfaces follow from [F2] by the fixed map $T(z)=(1/2,1/2)+z/4$, whose image lies in $(0,1)^2$. In two dimensions this map preserves the Dirichlet energy, while its $H^1$ norm satisfies $\tfrac14\|v\|_{H^1(D_1)}\le\|v\circ T^{-1}\|_{H^1(T(D_1))}\le\|v\|_{H^1(D_1)}$. Thus weak solutions, constant quotients and bounded energy DN maps transport with fixed norm-equivalence constants. The equality between the full and constant-quotient norms also follows directly from the double-annihilation argument in [F2]. Let $U=u_2(z,k)$ and $V=\overline{u_1(z,-k)}$. Both solve their respective conductivity equations weakly, and both are smooth and harmonic near and outside $\partial D_1$, because the coefficients equal one there. The boundary Wronskian $W=\int_{\partial D_1}(U\partial_\nu V-V\partial_\nu U)\,ds$ therefore equals the bilinear DN pairing $\int_{\partial D_1}V(\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})U\,ds$, using symmetry and the weak energy definition in [F2]. This identity also follows without assuming interior smoothness: subtract the weak energy forms, whose restrictions to a harmonic boundary collar are the classical fluxes. On every exterior circle $|z|=R>1$, the Wronskian has this same value by [F3].

Write the exterior holomorphic pieces of $U$ as $e^{ikz}A_2(z,k)$ and of $V$ as $e^{-ikz}J_1(z,-k)$; the other two pieces are antiholomorphic. Cross Wronskians between a holomorphic and an antiholomorphic piece integrate to zero: their integrand is $i$ or $-i$ times the tangential derivative of their product. The holomorphic–holomorphic contribution is $2\pi$ times the $z^{-1}$ coefficient of $A_2\partial_zJ_1-J_1\partial_zA_2-2ikA_2J_1$, hence equals $-4\pi ik\overline{\tau_1(-k)}$. To check the circle factor, $\partial_\nu H=(z/R)H'$ for a holomorphic function and $dz=iz\,ds/R$, so its Wronskian integral is $(1/i)$ times the contour integral. The antiholomorphic–antiholomorphic contribution is similarly $4\pi i\overline k\tau_2(k)$; its contour runs clockwise in $\overline z$. Thus $W=4\pi i[\overline k\tau_2(k)-k\overline{\tau_1(-k)}]$. This calculation uses only the Laurent coefficients in [F1]; all derivative product terms start at order $z^{-2}$ and do not contribute.

Apply the same calculation with the two conductivities equal to $\gamma_1$. The boundary pairing in step 1.1 is then zero, so $k\overline{\tau_1(-k)}=\overline k\tau_1(k)$. Substituting this relation in step 2.1 gives $W=4\pi i\overline k(\tau_2(k)-\tau_1(k))$. By [F2], the absolute DN pairing is at most $\delta$ times the product of the two trace-class norms modulo constants. Subtract $1$ from each solution representative to bound these norms by the $H^1$ norms of $u_j(\cdot,\pm k)-1$. The uniform bound in [F1] therefore gives $4\pi|k||\tau_2(k)-\tau_1(k)|\le C\delta |k|^2e^{C(1+|k|)}$. Divide by $4\pi|k|$ and enlarge $C$. At $k=0$, both amplitudes are zero by their definition. Finally $|k|\le e^{|k|}$ gives the second stated bound.

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^2$ be a nonempty bounded connected smooth domain and let $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$. Let $\gamma_j$ be real conductivities, $m\le\gamma_j\le M$ almost everywhere, equal to $1$ outside $\Omega'$, with $0<m\le M$. Extend them by $1$ to the disk $B=(1/2,1/2)+D_1$. On each domain use the weak energy DN map with trace space $\mathcal D=H^1/H_0^1$ and quotient $E=\mathcal D/\mathbb C\mathbf1$. Denote the constant-quotient DN difference norms by $\delta_\Omega(\gamma_1,\gamma_2)$ and $\delta_B(\gamma_1,\gamma_2)$. Then
$$\delta_B(\gamma_1,\gamma_2)\le C\delta_\Omega(\gamma_1,\gamma_2),\qquad \delta_B(\gamma_1^{-1},\gamma_2^{-1})\le C\delta_B(\gamma_1,\gamma_2),$$
where $C$ depends only on $m,M$ and the fixed geometry. Translation of $B$ to $D_1$ preserves these norms. In particular both disk data differences are bounded by a constant times the original measurement error, and both Beltrami coefficients have support in $D_a$ after this translation for a fixed $a<1$.

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice and the domains and conductivities in the statement.

[F1] Positive bounded conductivities on a unit-cube subdomain give unique weak Dirichlet solutions, bounded energy DN maps killing constants, and the rough Alessandrini identity with the exact full/constant-quotient operator norm equality. The trace quotient is the boundary trace space. ([[lem-ip-calderon-rough-dn-map-wellposedness]], [[lem-ip-calderon-rough-alessandrini-and-quotient-norm]], [[lem-ip-calderon-boundary-trace-quotient-identification]])

[F2] Poincaré–Wirtinger holds on convex domains with a constant bounded by a dimensional constant times their diameter. Bounded coercive forms on Hilbert spaces are invertible by Lax–Milgram. ([[cor-poincare-wirtinger-on-convex-domains]], [[thm-lax-milgram]])

[F3] Circle Fourier modes are complete and obey Parseval; smooth ambient restrictions are dense in $H^1$ of a smooth domain. The Sobolev Green formula identifies weak normal and tangential boundary functionals by approximation. ([[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], [[thm-smooth-up-to-the-boundary-density-on-smooth-domains]], [[thm-sobolev-gauss-green-formula-on-c-one-domains]])

[F4] Interior mollification is smooth, commutes with weak derivatives, and converges in $L^2$ on compact subdomains. ([[thm-convolution-with-a-mollifier-is-smooth-and-differentiates-under-the-integral-sign]], [[thm-l-one-approximate-identities-converge-in-l-p]])

proof_rows.text: Disk weak solutions in [F1] are obtained by an explicit fixed affine transport into the unit cube: $T(z)=(1/2,1/2)+z/4$ on $D_1$. In two dimensions this preserves the gradient energy and changes the $L^2$ term by a factor $1/16$, so $\tfrac14\|v\|_{H^1(D_1)}\le\|v\circ T^{-1}\|_{H^1(T(D_1))}\le\|v\|_{H^1(D_1)}$. Thus the disk weak solution estimate and DN boundedness follow with uniform constants, using ellipticity bounds $m_*:=\min\{m,1\}$ and $M_*:=\max\{M,1\}$ for the extended coefficients. The algebra proving the Alessandrini identity and double-annihilation norm equality in [F1] is invariant under this transport. Translation is an $H^1$ isometry, so it transports $B$ and its quotient DN map isometrically to $D_1$.

For trace classes $f,g$ on $B$, let $u_1,u_2$ solve the two conductivity equations there. Their restrictions to $\Omega$ are the respective weak solutions for their own restricted traces. Since the coefficient difference is zero on $B\setminus\Omega$, applying the Alessandrini identity on the two domains gives $((\Lambda_{\gamma_1}^{B}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2}^{B})f)(g)=((\Lambda_{\gamma_1}^{\Omega}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2}^{\Omega})[u_1|_\Omega])([u_2|_\Omega])$. In the sesquilinear convention this is exactly the common integral of $(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)\nabla u_1\cdot\overline{\nabla u_2}$. Its absolute value is at most $\delta_\Omega\|u_1\|_{H^1(B)}\|u_2\|_{H^1(B)}\le C\delta_\Omega\|f\|_{\mathcal D(B)}\|g\|_{\mathcal D(B)}$, using step 1.1. Hence the full disk operator norm is at most $C\delta_\Omega$, and its constant-quotient norm is equal to that full norm by [F1]. This proves the first estimate.

On $D_1$ let $E=\mathcal D/\mathbb C\mathbf1$ and let $D$ be the weak counterclockwise tangential derivative on its boundary. This is a bounded bijection $E\to E^*$ with bounded inverse. For completeness, the squared $E$ norm of a finite boundary Fourier sum $\sum_{n\ne0}a_ne^{in\theta}$ is comparable to $2\pi\sum|n||a_n|^2$. The lower bound follows from the minimum Dirichlet energy of the harmonic lift $\sum a_nr^{|n|}e^{in\theta}$: subtracting that lift from any representative leaves a zero-trace function, whose gradient is orthogonal to the harmonic lift. Its energy is $2\pi\sum|n||a_n|^2$. The lift's squared $L^2$ norm is $\pi\sum|a_n|^2/(|n|+1)$, which gives the upper bound for the quotient norm. Finite modes are dense in $E$: angular Fourier projections converge in $H^1(D_1)$ by polar Parseval first for smooth ambient restrictions, and then for general functions by [F3]; their quotient traces are the finite boundary modes. In these equivalent weighted sequence norms, $D$ multiplies the $n$th coefficient by $in$, and the dual norm uses weight $1/|n|$. This proves its bounded invertibility.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix $B,C>0$ and $0<b<1$. Let $g\in C^1(\mathbb C;\mathbb C)$, let $\ell\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, and suppose $g(0)=0$ and
$$|g(k)-\ell k|\le C|k|^{1-b}\qquad(|k|\ge1).$$
Suppose distributionally $\bar\partial g=\sigma g+E$, where $\sigma$ is measurable, $\|\sigma\|_\infty\le B$, $E\in C^1$, and for $0<\delta\le1/2$,
$$|E(k)|\le C\delta e^{C|k|},\qquad |\nabla E(k)|\le C e^{C(1+|k|)}.$$
There exist $D>0$ and $\delta_0\in(0,1/2)$, depending only on $B,C,b$, such that
$$|\ell|\ge D[\log(1/\delta)]^{-b},\quad0<\delta<\delta_0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad g(k)\ne0\text{ for every }k\ne0.$$
If $E=0$, the same conclusion holds for every $\ell\ne0$, without a threshold condition.

The constants for a support disk of radius $R\ge1$ grow at most as a fixed power of $R$, by dilation to a fixed disk. [F2] A distribution with zero $\bar\partial$ derivative is holomorphic: applying $\partial$ makes it harmonic, so Weyl regularity applies and the Cauchy–Riemann equation concludes. A holomorphic function's boundary winding counts its zeros with multiplicity; winding is invariant under nonvanishing homotopy. A nonvanishing holomorphic function satisfies the minimum-modulus principle. ([[thm-weyl-lemma-for-the-laplacian]], [[thm-argument-principle-as-image-winding-number]], [[cor-winding-number-classifies-loops-in-the-punctured-plane]], [[thm-minimum-modulus-principle]])

proof_rows.text: Set $\lambda=|\ell|$ and choose $R=\max\{1,(8C/\lambda)^{1/b}\}$. Then for $|k|\ge R$, $|g(k)-\ell k|\le(\lambda/8)|k|$, so $g$ is nonzero there and its restriction to $|k|=R$ has winding one, by the straight homotopy to $\ell k$. Choose a smooth real cutoff $\chi_R$ equal to $1$ on $D_R$, supported in $D_{2R}$, with derivative bounded by $C/R$, and set $s=\mathcal C(\sigma\chi_R)$. Direct integration of its kernel gives $\|s\|_\infty\le C_B R$. The $L^4$ Cauchy estimate in [F1] gives a one-half Hölder bound at most $C_B R^{1/2}$. These estimates hold independently of the regularity of $\sigma$.

Put $H=e^{-s}E\chi_R$ and $S=\mathcal CH-\mathcal CH(0)$. On $D_{2R}$ the hypotheses give $\|E\|_\infty\le C\delta e^{2CR}$ and $\operatorname{Lip}(E)\le Ce^{C(1+2R)}$. The elementary estimate $|E(x)-E(y)|\le\min\{2\|E\|_\infty,\operatorname{Lip}(E)|x-y|\}$ implies $[E]_{C^{0,1/2}}\le C\delta^{1/2}e^{C'R}$ on that disk. Combine this with step 1.1 and the cutoff product estimate to get $\|H\|_{C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb C)}\le C\delta^{1/2}e^{C'R}$; the smooth cutoff vanishes before leaving $D_{2R}$, so extension by zero retains this bound after increasing the constant. By [F1] and dilation, $\|\nabla S\|_\infty\le C\delta^{1/2}e^{C_1R}$, absorbing polynomial powers of $R$ into the exponential. Also $S(0)=0$, so $|S(k)|\le C\delta^{1/2}e^{C_1R}|k|$. If $E=0$, take $S=0$ and these bounds hold with zero right side.

Define $F=e^{-s}g-S$. The distributional product rule, justified by the locally Sobolev Cauchy gauge and smooth approximation, gives $\bar\partial F=e^{-s}(1-\chi_R)(\sigma g+E)$, hence $F$ is holomorphic on $D_R$ by [F2], and $F(0)=0$. Suppose $C\delta^{1/2}e^{(C_1+C_B)R}\le\lambda/8$. On $|k|=R$, step 1.1 gives $|e^{-s}g|\ge(7/8)\lambda R e^{-C_BR}$ and step 2.1 makes $|S|\le(1/8)\lambda R e^{-C_BR}$. Thus $F$ is homotopic there to $e^{-s}g$, whose winding is one: $e^{-s}$ has a continuous logarithm on the disk, so contributes winding zero. By [F2], $F$ has precisely one zero counted with multiplicity in $D_R$. Since $F(0)=0$, it is simple and there are no others. Consequently $F(k)/k$ extends holomorphically and nonvanishingly to $D_R$ and its boundary, where its modulus is at least $(3/4)\lambda e^{-C_BR}$. The minimum-modulus principle gives the same lower bound throughout. Step 2.1 now yields $|F(k)+S(k)|\ge(5/8)\lambda e^{-C_BR}|k|$ for $0<|k|<R$. Hence $g=e^s(F+S)$ has no zero except zero inside this disk, and step 1.1 excludes all the exterior zeros. If $E=0$, the same proof works for every $\lambda>0$.

It remains to ensure the displayed smallness condition. Write $L=\log(1/\delta)$. If $\lambda\ge DL^{-b}$, then $R\le1+(8C/D)^{1/b}L$. Choose $D$ large enough that $(C_1+C_B)(8C/D)^{1/b}\le1/4$. For large $L$, the left side of the smallness condition is at most $C'e^{-L/4}$, while its right side is at least $(D/8)L^{-b}$. Since $e^{-L/4}L^b\to0$, there is a fixed $L_0$ for which the condition holds whenever $L\ge L_0$. Put $\delta_0=\min\{1/4,e^{-L_0}\}$. Step 3.1 then proves the asserted implication and its zero-error version.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^2$ be a nonempty bounded connected smooth domain, let $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, and fix $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$ and $R>0$. For every $\gamma,\gamma_0\in X_2(R)$ there exist constants $C>0$, $\rho>0$ and $t_0\in(0,1)$, depending only on $\Omega,\Omega',m,M,R$, such that
$$\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C\,\omega\!\left(\|\dot{\Lambda}_\gamma-\dot{\Lambda}_{\gamma_0}\|_{\mathcal L(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1,(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1)^*)}\right),$$
where $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ is the trace quotient and $\dot\Lambda_\gamma$ is the induced weak Dirichlet-to-Neumann map on the constant quotient, and
$$\omega(0):=0,\qquad \omega(t):=\left[\log\!\left(\frac1{\min\{t,t_0\}}\right)\right]^{-\rho}\quad(t>0).$$

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, the fixed domain, collar and class parameters in the statement, and $\gamma_1=\gamma$, $\gamma_2=\gamma_0\in X_2(R)$.

[F1] The background extensions of the BV class have uniform $L^p$ translation difference bounds $C_pt^{1/p}$ for every sufficiently large finite $p$. ([[def-ip-calderon-admissible-conductivity-class]], [[lem-ip-bv-translation-modulus-for-conductivity]])

[F2] Enclosing the domain in the fixed disk $B=(1/2,1/2)+D_1$, extending the coefficients by $1$, and translating to $D_1$ controls both the disk DN difference and the reciprocal-conductivity disk DN difference by a constant times the original constant-quotient DN norm. The supports of their Beltrami coefficients lie in a fixed $D_a$, $a<1$. ([[def-ip-calderon-weak-dn-map-for-bounded-conductivities]], [[lem-ip-calderon-boundary-trace-quotient-identification]], [[lem-ip-calderon-rough-dn-map-wellposedness]], [[lem-ip-planar-dn-enclosure-and-reciprocal-comparison]])

[F3] Measurable Beltrami coefficients give normalized solutions $f_\mu$, principal quasiconformal phases, uniform local $W^{1,r}$ bounds and inverse-gradient $L^{r-2}$ bounds at $|k|=1$. Under a uniform positive power translation modulus, their conductivity CGO combinations $u_\gamma=e^{\delta_\gamma}$ have continuous onto logarithmic phases and satisfy $|\delta_\gamma(z,k)-ikz|\le C|k|^{1-b}$ for $|k|\ge1$, uniformly in $z$, for some $b>0$. On fixed disks the $u_\gamma(\cdot,1)$ have a uniform positive Hölder exponent. ([[lem-ip-planar-measurable-beltrami-cgo-solutions]], [[lem-ip-planar-beltrami-cgo-power-phase-decay]], [[lem-ip-planar-conductivity-cgo-logarithmic-phases]])

[F4] The scattering amplitudes obey $|\tau_\mu|\le1$, $\bar\partial_k\delta_\gamma=-i\tau_\mu e^{\overline\delta_\gamma-\delta_\gamma}$, and uniform exponential bounds on their parameter derivatives and those of $\delta_\gamma(z,k)$ for bounded $z$. Their difference is at most $C\delta e^{C(1+|k|)}$ in terms of the disk DN difference. ([[lem-ip-planar-scattering-dbar-equation-and-parameter-bounds]], [[lem-ip-planar-dn-to-scattering-lipschitz-estimate]])

[F5] If $g(0)=0$, $g(k)=\ell k+O(|k|^{1-b})$, and $\bar\partial g=\sigma g+E$ with $\sigma$ uniformly bounded, $|E|\le C\varepsilon e^{C|k|}$ and $|\nabla E|\le Ce^{C(1+|k|)}$, then $|\ell|\ge D[\log(1/\varepsilon)]^{-b}$ excludes every nonzero zero of $g$ for sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$. If $E=0$, every $\ell\ne0$ excludes them. ([[lem-ip-planar-scattering-topological-zero-separation]])

[F6] Uniform power translation bounds for $\mu_j$, fixed-parameter $W^{1,r}$ bounds for $f_j$, and uniform negative-gradient integrability imply $\|\gamma_1-\gamma_2\|_2\le C\|f_1-f_2\|_{L^\infty(D_2)}^\eta$ for some $\eta>0$, including zero error. This is proved by Caccioppoli, frequency splitting and interpolation. ([[lem-ip-planar-conductivity-l2-interpolation]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are assumed in the quoted BV, weak-solution, quasiconformal and Fourier interfaces. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

proof_rows.text: Extend both coefficients by $1$ and use the fixed translation in [F2]. Let $K=\max\{2,M,m^{-1}\}$, $\kappa=(K-1)/(K+1)\in(0,1)$, and $\mu_j=(1-\gamma_j)/(1+\gamma_j)$. Then $|\mu_j|\le\kappa$ and their support lies in $D_a$. The scalar function $x\mapsto(1-x)/(1+x)$ is Lipschitz on $[\min\{m,1\},\max\{M,1\}]$, so [F1] gives $\omega_p(\mu_j,t)\le C_pt^{1/p}$ for all sufficiently large finite $p$. Choose $2<r\le p_\kappa$ sufficiently close to $2$ that $q=2r/(r-2)$ and $p=2q=4r/(r-2)$ both lie in this range. These are fixed class-dependent exponents. The same bounds apply to $-\mu_j$, which correspond to the reciprocal conductivities. Thus all hypotheses of [F3]–[F6] hold uniformly for both conductivity pairs, and [F2] bounds both corresponding disk measurement errors by $C\varepsilon$.

For either of these two pairs, write the conductivity phases as $\delta_j$ and amplitudes as $\tau_j$. Fix $z\in D_2$ and any $w\in\mathbb C$, and put $g(k)=\delta_1(z,k)-\delta_2(w,k)$. Then $g(0)=0$ and $g(k)=i(z-w)k+O(|k|^{1-b})$ by [F3], with a constant independent of $z,w$. The phase equation in [F4] gives $\bar\partial_kg=\sigma g+E$, where, when $g\ne0$, $\sigma=-i\tau_2[e^{\overline\delta_1-\delta_1}-e^{\overline\delta_2-\delta_2}]/g$, and set $\sigma=0$ where $g=0$; also $E=-i(\tau_1-\tau_2)e^{\overline\delta_1-\delta_1}$. Since these exponentials have modulus one and the exponential is Lipschitz on the imaginary axis, $|\sigma|\le2|\tau_2|\le2$. By [F2]–[F4], $|E|\le C\varepsilon e^{C|k|}$ after increasing $C$, and $|\nabla_kE|\le Ce^{C(1+|k|)}$: differentiate the amplitude difference and the unit-modulus exponential, using only the parameter derivative bound for $\delta_1(z,k)$ with $z\in D_2$. This last estimate is independent of $w$. Thus [F5] applies with $\ell=i(z-w)$. If necessary reduce $b$ below $1$; this only weakens the already proved phase bound.

At the fixed parameter $k=1$, surjectivity of $\delta_2(\cdot,1)$ in [F3] supplies a point $w$ with $\delta_2(w,1)=\delta_1(z,1)$. For sufficiently small $0<\varepsilon<t_0$, step 2.1 and [F5] force $|z-w|<D[\log(1/\varepsilon)]^{-b}$. Reduce $t_0$ so this distance is below one; then $w\in D_3$. The uniform Hölder continuity from [F3], with exponent $\theta_0=1-2/r>0$, gives $|u_1(z,1)-u_2(z,1)|=|u_2(w,1)-u_2(z,1)|\le C|w-z|^{\theta_0}\le C[\log(1/\varepsilon)]^{-b\theta_0}$. The bound holds uniformly for $z\in D_2$, and for both the original and reciprocal pairs. If $\varepsilon=0$, the amplitude differences in [F4] vanish, so $E=0$ and the zero-error clause of [F5] forces $w=z$. In that case both conductivity CGO pairs agree exactly.

By the definition of the two conductivity combinations, $f_{\mu_j}(z,1)=\operatorname{Re}u_{\gamma_j}(z,1)+i\operatorname{Im}u_{\gamma_j^{-1}}(z,1)$. Applying step 3.1 to the two pairs therefore gives $\|f_{\mu_1}(\cdot,1)-f_{\mu_2}(\cdot,1)\|_{L^\infty(D_2)}\le C[\log(1/\varepsilon)]^{-b\theta_0}$ for small positive $\varepsilon$, and zero difference when $\varepsilon=0$. At this fixed parameter, [F3] gives the uniform $W^{1,r}(D_3)$ bound and the inverse-gradient integral with $\sigma=r-2>0$. The coefficient modulus needed in [F6] is $\omega_q(\mu_j,t)\le C_qt^{1/q}$ from step 1.1. Reduce $t_0$ so the displayed solution difference is at most one, as required by [F6].

Apply [F6] with its modulus exponent $\theta=1/q$ and inverse-gradient exponent $\sigma=r-2$. Its positive exponent is $\eta=\theta\sigma/[(1+\theta)(2+\sigma)]$. Step 4.1 yields $\|\gamma_1-\gamma_2\|_{L^2(D_1)}\le C[\log(1/\varepsilon)]^{-\rho}$, with $\rho=b\theta_0\eta>0$, for $0<\varepsilon<t_0$. The translated coefficient difference vanishes outside the original $\Omega$, so this is exactly its $L^2(\Omega)$ norm. If $\varepsilon=0$, step 4.1 and the zero-error clause of [F6] give equality of the coefficients and the required value $\omega(0)=0$. Finally, for $\varepsilon\ge t_0$, use $\|\gamma_1-\gamma_2\|_2\le2M|\Omega|^{1/2}$ and enlarge $C$ to at least $2M|\Omega|^{1/2}[\log(1/t_0)]^\rho$. Taking $t_0<1$ yields precisely the saturated modulus in the statement. All exponents and constants were fixed using only the listed class and geometry parameters.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For each fixed integer $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected smooth domain, let $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, fix $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$, $R>0$ and $0<\alpha<1$, and let $\gamma,\gamma_0\in X_d(R)$. Set
$$\delta:=\|\dot{\Lambda}_\gamma-\dot{\Lambda}_{\gamma_0}\|_{\mathcal L(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1,(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1)^*)}.$$
There exist constants $C>0$, $\rho>0$ and $t_0\in(0,1)$, depending only on $d,\alpha,\Omega,\Omega',m,M,R$, such that
$$\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C\,\omega(\delta),\qquad \omega(0):=0,\qquad \omega(t):=\left[\log\!\left(\frac1{\min\{t,t_0\}}\right)\right]^{-\rho}\quad(t>0).$$
Here $X_d(R)$ is the BV class when $d=2$ and the bounded $C^{1,\alpha}$ class when $d\ge3$, and $\dot\Lambda_\gamma$ is the induced weak conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map on the trace quotient by constants.

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice; a fixed $d\ge2$ and the domain and parameters in the statement; $\gamma,\gamma_0\in X_d(R)$; and $\delta$ as defined there.

[F1] $X_2(R)$ is the real conductivity class with $m\le\gamma\le M$, background value $1$ outside $\Omega'$, and the stated BV norm bound; for $d\ge3$, $X_d(R)$ has the stated $C^{1,\alpha}$ bound. ([[def-ip-calderon-admissible-conductivity-class]])

[F2] $\Lambda_\gamma$ is the weak energy-form DN map, is well-defined and bounded on the trace quotient, kills constants and has range functionals annihilating constants; $\dot\Lambda_\gamma$ is its induced bounded map on the constant quotient. ([[def-ip-calderon-weak-dn-map-for-bounded-conductivities]], [[lem-ip-calderon-rough-dn-map-wellposedness]], [[lem-ip-calderon-boundary-trace-quotient-identification]])

[L1] In dimension $2$, every pair in $X_2(R)$ satisfies an $L^2$ logarithmic stability bound with positive exponent and a positive threshold, including the zero-data case. ([[lem-ip-calderon-planar-beltrami-dbar-logarithmic-stability]])

[L2] In dimensions $d\ge3$, every pair in $X_d(R)$ satisfies an $L^2$ logarithmic stability bound with positive exponent and a positive threshold, including the zero-data case. ([[lem-ip-calderon-higher-dimensional-cgo-fourier-logarithmic-stability]])

proof_rows.text: If $d=2$, apply [L1] and write its constants as $C_2,\rho_2,t_2$. If $d\ge3$, apply [L2] and write its constants as $C_d,\rho_d,t_d$. In either case, for the fixed dimension there are $C_*>0$, $\rho_*>0$, and $t_*>0$ such that $\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_2\le C_*[\log(1/\min\{\delta,t_*\})]^{-\rho_*}$ when $\delta>0$, and equality of the DN maps implies $\gamma=\gamma_0$.

Set $\rho:=\rho_*$ and $t_0:=\min\{t_*,1/2\}$. If $0<\delta<t_0$, then $\min\{\delta,t_0\}=\delta$ and $\min\{\delta,t_*\}=\delta$, so step 1.1 is exactly the asserted estimate with constant $C_*$. If $\delta=0$, step 1.1 gives $\gamma=\gamma_0$, so the estimate holds with $\omega(0)=0$.

If $\delta\ge t_0$, [F1] gives $\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_2\le2M|\Omega|^{1/2}$, while $\omega(\delta)=[\log(1/t_0)]^{-\rho}>0$. Choose $C\ge\max\{C_*,2M|\Omega|^{1/2}[\log(1/t_0)]^{\rho}\}$. Then the desired inequality follows for $\delta\ge t_0$ by this uniform coefficient bound and for $\delta<t_0$ by step 2.1. The constants have only the listed class and geometry dependence.
